messages.body_plain:
I added the Kim, Shephard and Chib (1998) model
as an example.  You can see the model(s) and the R
code to generate and test on simulated data in:

    src/models/misc/moving-avg/

You can browse these on the web through GitHub:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/master/src/models/misc/moving-avg

There is a straightforward implementation and a much
more efficient version with faster convergence (tens of samples versus
hundreds), better mixing, and faster iterations.

We need to reorganize our example models, so they probably
won't be on the above (slightly confusing) path forever.
I did add a section to the time-series chapter of the manual
describing the model, its conversion to Stan, and its
optimization.

Comments on these models or suggestions for other illustrative
models gladly accepted.  I'm trying to keep the examples simple,
so I'm not mixing autoregression and stochastic volatility in
the model as Carlos did in the original post.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Bob. I must say I'm incredibly impressed with how well the software works already, though - early stage academic software isn't supposed to be this good!

On another note, I did some benchmarking to see how long the various checks take for the multi_normal_prec() implementation. If I comment out all the checks for multi_normal_prec_log (i.e. lines 552-584 and 663-695) it results in about a 25% speed up. But using the code Ben helped with a couple weeks ago to use lp__ directly is even faster, about 50% faster than multi_normal_prec(). So I'm guessing there's some additional overhead in the multi_normal_prec() function that slows it down a bit. Of course they're all much, much faster than the basic multi_normal() which uses the covariance matrix.

Sampling times for 10k iterations:
multi_normal()                      1190s
multi_normal_prec()                 61s
multi_normal_prec with no checks    47s
lp__ method                         32s

Anyhow, just wanted to post that for reference in case anyone else is trying to optimize multivariate normals in their models. For my purposes, I'll probably stick with the basic multi_normal_prec() during development and then swap in the lp__ method instead when I'm doing big runs.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mode-jumping
messages.body_plain:
By default, Stan is attempting to sample from the posterior distribution. It does not provide a point estimate (like optimization) or an approximation of your posterior distribution (algorithms like EP or VB). If there are multiple modes in the posterior, than Stan, like any other correct MCMC algorithm, "should" sample from the posterior in the limit. Have you taken a look at some of the built-in convergence diagnostics, split R-hat and estimated number of effective samples? Have you visualized the samples themselves? (The alternative is to just look at the output of print.) If you haven't, that's the place to start.

With regards to non-identifiable models, there are sections in the manual that discuss this issue and some suggestions on how to deal with it. I would also recommend the Gelman and Hill book on multilevel models.

So, the answer you're looking for is yes. But since Stan's default sampling algorithm, NUTS, isn't trying to search for a mode, there is no concept of turning mode-jumping on or off.

Hopefully that helps.

Daniel

tempering or ensemble methods to help with mode jumping.
Nor is anything like this going to be added in the near
future unless someone volunteers and implements it for us.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning random effects to observations
messages.body_plain:
Comments inlined.

On 4/1/13 9:21 PM, Kyle Foreman wrote:
> Hello again all,
>
> I'm playing around with a model that has a random effect for each US state, with seven observations over time for each
> state. So, there's a vector of 51 random effects in a GMRF/CAR structure (based off of the GeoBUGS lip cancer model I've
> discussed on the list previously), and they in turn need to be factored into the likelihoods of 357 datapoints.
>
> I've tried a few different methods and am curious as to what you'd recommend as the best method for Stan.
>
> The first thing I tried was just looping through each observation to add in its random effects, as one would do in BUGS
> (attached as CAR_model_loop.stan.txt):
>
> |
> for (n in 1:N) {
>      s <- state[n];
>      beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[s];
> }
> |
>
> this works, but I thought I should try to vectorize if possible and remove the loop.
>
> So next (in CAR_model_matrix.stan.txt) I built a binary matrix[357,51] that when multiplied by beta_stz[51] gives the
> filled in random effects for each observation:
>
> |
> matrix[N,S] state_mat;
> for (n in 1:N)
>      for (s in 1:S)
>          state_mat[n,s] <- if_else(state[n]==s, 1.0, 0.0);
> |
>
> |
> beta1_long <- state_mat * beta1_stz;
> |
>
> I was surprised to find this takes about 3x longer than the looping version.

Loops are very very fast in Stan -- they just get compiled to
C++ and most modern CPUs can easily parallelize the integer arithmetic
and comparisons in the loop and any floating point/assignments within
the loop.

The matrix operations are relatively slow because it's doing a ton of
extra work because of the sparsity.

We are going to add sparse matrix data types eventually, at which point
the matrix version might be faster.

The real issue is whether the operations are working exclusively
on variables declared in data or transformed data, or whether
they involve parameters (parameter, transformed parameter, local
variable in transformed parameter, or local variable in model block).

With parameters, so-called "reduction" operations that have a single
output are much faster when vectorized because we can vectorize the gradient calc,
which is otherwise slow.

So if either x or y is a parameter or transformed parameter of a local
variable declared in the model or transformed parameter

vector[N] x;
vector[N] y;
real sum;
...
sum <- 0;

for (n in 1:N)

    sum <- sum + x[n] * y[n];

is much slower than

    sum <- x' * y;

which is in turn a little bit slower than

    sum <- dot_product(x,y);

On the other hand, you won't see much difference
between:

   z <- exp(x);

and

   for (n in 1:N)

     z[n] <- exp(x[n]);

because we can't vectorize the gradients because of the
multiple outputs for z[n], which need to be stored and
reasoned about independently.

> In PyMC I've always found a slight speedup using the matrix version. And by switching to sparse matrix libraries for
> state_mat in python I get an order of magnitude further speedup or more.

That's because loops are slow in Python (unless you're using
something like Cython that compiles them to C++).

> Any suggestions on how to best handle these types of operations in Stan? Thanks again!

I hope that helps.  If not, please keep asking questions!

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
As Ben first pointed out, the problem here is the
following material which g++ can't (and shouldn't be asked to)
interpret:

   ... [1] LC_CTYPE=C;LC_NUMERIC=C;LC_TIME=C;LC_COLLATE=C;LC_MONETARY=C;LC_MESSAGES=en_US.UTF-8;LC_PAPER=C;LC_NAME=C;
   LC_ADDRESS=C;LC_TELEPHONE=C;LC_MEASUREMENT=en_US.UTF-8;LC_IDENTIFICATION=C

g++ balks when it gets to [1], which it can't interpret.
None of this material should be passed to g++.  You need to
figure out where it's coming from (hint: those values don't originate
in Stan) and get rid of it.

It appears to somehow be related to locales:

   http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/locale/LC_categories

but the above is not the way to set properties on the command
line.  The semicolons give it away, which will be interpreted
as end-of-command marks.

So it looks like g++ may be picking up wrongly-specified environment variables
somewhere.  If you can look at your global environment variables, you
might be able to see where that is.  Or Jiqiang may know what's getting included
in the call to g++ after the .o files and be able to give you a hint.  Or you might
be able to do a global search (grep -R if you have to from /) on your computer to find
where these values are  defined.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning random effects to observations
messages.body_plain:
Thanks so much, Bob! I always like to learn more about what's going on under the hood. I haven't worked with C++ much til now and hadn't realized it automatically parallelized loops like that - good to know.

On Tue, Apr 2, 2013 at 12:44 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Comments inlined.
>
>
> On 4/1/13 9:21 PM, Kyle Foreman wrote:
> > Hello again all,
> >
> > I'm playing around with a model that has a random effect for each US state, with seven observations over time for each
> > state. So, there's a vector of 51 random effects in a GMRF/CAR structure (based off of the GeoBUGS lip cancer model I've
> > discussed on the list previously), and they in turn need to be factored into the likelihoods of 357 datapoints.
> >
> > I've tried a few different methods and am curious as to what you'd recommend as the best method for Stan.
> >
> > The first thing I tried was just looping through each observation to add in its random effects, as one would do in BUGS
> > (attached as CAR_model_loop.stan.txt):
> >
> > |
> > for (n in 1:N) {
> >      s <- state[n];
> >      beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[s];
> > }
> > |
> >
> > this works, but I thought I should try to vectorize if possible and remove the loop.
> >
> > So next (in CAR_model_matrix.stan.txt) I built a binary matrix[357,51] that when multiplied by beta_stz[51] gives the
> > filled in random effects for each observation:
> >
> > |
> > matrix[N,S] state_mat;
> > for (n in 1:N)
> >      for (s in 1:S)
> >          state_mat[n,s] <- if_else(state[n]==s, 1.0, 0.0);
> > |
> >
> > |
> > beta1_long <- state_mat * beta1_stz;
> > |
> >
> > I was surprised to find this takes about 3x longer than the looping version.
>
> Loops are very very fast in Stan -- they just get compiled to
> C++ and most modern CPUs can easily parallelize the integer arithmetic
> and comparisons in the loop and any floating point/assignments within
> the loop.
>
> The matrix operations are relatively slow because it's doing a ton of
> extra work because of the sparsity.
>
> We are going to add sparse matrix data types eventually, at which point
> the matrix version might be faster.
>
> The real issue is whether the operations are working exclusively
> on variables declared in data or transformed data, or whether
> they involve parameters (parameter, transformed parameter, local
> variable in transformed parameter, or local variable in model block).
>
> With parameters, so-called "reduction" operations that have a single
> output are much faster when vectorized because we can vectorize the gradient calc,
> which is otherwise slow.
>
> So if either x or y is a parameter or transformed parameter of a local
> variable declared in the model or transformed parameter
>
> vector[N] x;
> vector[N] y;
> real sum;
> ...
> sum <- 0;
>
> for (n in 1:N)
>    sum <- sum + x[n] * y[n];
>
> is much slower than
>
>    sum <- x' * y;
>
> which is in turn a little bit slower than
>
>    sum <- dot_product(x,y);
>
>
> On the other hand, you won't see much difference
> between:
>
>   z <- exp(x);
>
> and
>
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     z[n] <- exp(x[n]);
>
> because we can't vectorize the gradients because of the
> multiple outputs for z[n], which need to be stored and
> reasoned about independently.
>
>
> > In PyMC I've always found a slight speedup using the matrix version. And by switching to sparse matrix libraries for
> > state_mat in python I get an order of magnitude further speedup or more.
>
> That's because loops are slow in Python (unless you're using
> something like Cython that compiles them to C++).
>
>
> > Any suggestions on how to best handle these types of operations in Stan? Thanks again!
>
> I hope that helps.  If not, please keep asking questions!
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning random effects to observations
messages.body_plain:
It's not just C++ and it's not just loops.  Modern
compilers try to execute a pipeline of instructions in
parallel.  The biggest performance costs are for branches
that can't be predicted and expensive operations like
math lib calls or even division.

A good compiler can help lay out instructions to make
the CPU's job easier.

If you want to know more, Agner Fog's free online book on
optimizing C++ is great and it discusses both hardware and C++
in particular:

   http://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf

Just don't take the comments about the evils of templates too
seriously.

We've tried to be fairly careful in laying out Stan, but
there's a lot of room for improvement, and we're getting
some expert help in that direction.

- Bob

On 4/3/13 12:53 AM, Kyle Foreman wrote:
> Thanks so much, Bob! I always like to learn more about what's going on under the hood. I haven't worked with C++ much
> til now and hadn't realized it automatically parallelized loops like that - good to know.
>
>
> On Tue, Apr 2, 2013 at 12:44 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
>     Comments inlined.
>
>
>     On 4/1/13 9:21 PM, Kyle Foreman wrote:
>
>         Hello again all,
>
>         I'm playing around with a model that has a random effect for each US state, with seven observations over time
>         for each
>         state. So, there's a vector of 51 random effects in a GMRF/CAR structure (based off of the GeoBUGS lip cancer
>         model I've
>         discussed on the list previously), and they in turn need to be factored into the likelihoods of 357 datapoints.
>
>         I've tried a few different methods and am curious as to what you'd recommend as the best method for Stan.
>
>         The first thing I tried was just looping through each observation to add in its random effects, as one would do
>         in BUGS
>         (attached as CAR_model_loop.stan.txt):
>
>         |
>         for (n in 1:N) {
>               s <- state[n];
>               beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[s];
>         }
>         |
>
>         this works, but I thought I should try to vectorize if possible and remove the loop.
>
>         So next (in CAR_model_matrix.stan.txt) I built a binary matrix[357,51] that when multiplied by beta_stz[51]
>         gives the
>         filled in random effects for each observation:
>
>         |
>         matrix[N,S] state_mat;
>         for (n in 1:N)
>               for (s in 1:S)
>                   state_mat[n,s] <- if_else(state[n]==s, 1.0, 0.0);
>         |
>
>         |
>         beta1_long <- state_mat * beta1_stz;
>         |
>
>         I was surprised to find this takes about 3x longer than the looping version.
>
>
>     Loops are very very fast in Stan -- they just get compiled to
>     C++ and most modern CPUs can easily parallelize the integer arithmetic
>     and comparisons in the loop and any floating point/assignments within
>     the loop.
>
>     The matrix operations are relatively slow because it's doing a ton of
>     extra work because of the sparsity.
>
>     We are going to add sparse matrix data types eventually, at which point
>     the matrix version might be faster.
>
>     The real issue is whether the operations are working exclusively
>     on variables declared in data or transformed data, or whether
>     they involve parameters (parameter, transformed parameter, local
>     variable in transformed parameter, or local variable in model block).
>
>     With parameters, so-called "reduction" operations that have a single
>     output are much faster when vectorized because we can vectorize the gradient calc,
>     which is otherwise slow.
>
>     So if either x or y is a parameter or transformed parameter of a local
>     variable declared in the model or transformed parameter
>
>     vector[N] x;
>     vector[N] y;
>     real sum;
>     ...
>     sum <- 0;
>
>     for (n in 1:N)
>         sum <- sum + x[n] * y[n];
>
>     is much slower than
>
>         sum <- x' * y;
>
>     which is in turn a little bit slower than
>
>         sum <- dot_product(x,y);
>
>
>     On the other hand, you won't see much difference
>     between:
>
>        z <- exp(x);
>
>     and
>
>
>        for (n in 1:N)
>          z[n] <- exp(x[n]);
>
>     because we can't vectorize the gradients because of the
>     multiple outputs for z[n], which need to be stored and
>     reasoned about independently.
>
>
>         In PyMC I've always found a slight speedup using the matrix version. And by switching to sparse matrix libraries for
>         state_mat in python I get an order of magnitude further speedup or more.
>
>
>     That's because loops are slow in Python (unless you're using
>     something like Cython that compiles them to C++).
>
>
>         Any suggestions on how to best handle these types of operations in Stan? Thanks again!
>
>
>     I hope that helps.  If not, please keep asking questions!
>
>     - Bob
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Yes, you can use an if statement in the transformed
data block.

But if the missing data is a parameter, then you need
to put the two together in the transformed parameter block.

So if your model's not compiling, there must be another
issue.  Could you send us the Stan code you're trying
to get working?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 4/4/13 8:09 PM, Kyle Foreman wrote:
>     If you want to know more, Agner Fog's free online book on
>     optimizing C++ is great and it discusses both hardware and C++
>     in particular:
>
>
> Thanks, Bob, adding that to the reading list!
>
> On a somewhat related note, when I'm generating interim quantities in a model like this, is there a way to store the
> final quantity but not the intermediate ones?

The only values saved during sampling are variables
declared in the parameters block, in the transformed parameters
block, or in the generated quantities block.

So define what you want to save in one of those blocks,
and define everything else as a local variable.

>
> For instance, I'd like to store the traces of log_mu
> |
> log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;
> |
>
> but I don't need beta1_long or beta1_stz
> |
> beta1_stz <- beta1 - mean(beta1);
> for (n in 1:N) {
>      beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[state[n]];
> |

That's fine.  Declare beta1_long and beta1_stz as local variables
and they won't be written out.  They can still be used to define
log_mu, and log_mu will still be visible outside the transformed
parameter block.

> In order to move log_mu from model to transformed parameters, I have to also put beta1_stz and beta1_long there.
> (Otherwise they're of course out of scope and log_mu can't be computed in transformed parameters).

Right.  Which means they won't be visible in the model
block.

> If I instead try to generate a new quantity from log_mu in generated quantities I get an error that log_mu doesn't
> exist, since it's local to the model block.
> |
> generated quantities {
>      vector[N] mu;
>      mu <- exp(log_mu);
> }
> |
>
> The only way I can think to save log_mu without also storing beta1_stz/beta1_long is to bypass them altogether, but that
> prevents vectorization:
> |
> transformed parameters {
>      vector[N] log_mu;
>      for (n in 1:N)
>          log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));
> }
> |

I'm not sure what you mean by "prevents vectorization".  What
gets saved is orthogonal to what's vectorized.

> Based on the manual and this thread <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/lybDQTpMWRw/QduePUFLcp0J> I'm guessing

> my only option is to also store the interim quantities by putting them all in the transformed parameters block. Is that
> accurate? Not a big deal for this model, just keeping an eye towards my eventual model which is huge...

Can you send a working model that perhaps saves too much
and indicate which variables you want to save?  It's hard
to tell from code fragments.

You can (re)define whatever you want in generated quantities and
it'll get saved.  The generated quantities are only computed
once per iteration, not once per leapfrog step, and they're
computed with double values rather than auto-dif variables for
gradients, so they're much faster.  The problem is that it
can require redundant definitions.

For example, you can add this to generated quantities and log_mu
will get saved:

   generated quantities {

     vector[N] log_mu;
     for (n in 1:N)
       log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));

That is, assuming everything on the right side is either data, a parameter,
or a transformed parameter.  If not, the values might be able to be
recomputed.

Loops involving only arithmetic on double values, like the above,
are very fast in Stan.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] efficiency of stan and mcmc methods in general
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] efficiency of stan and mcmc methods in general
messages.body_plain:
Stan's not going to be super fast in its current
incarnation for 1M data points, no matter what you do.
So if you want a regression fit in 3 minutes for
1M data points and 120 parameters, you're probably going
to have to look elsewhere.

But if your model makes sense, Stan should be able to
fit it, even with 1M data points.

I don't understand your model, but have some general
advice.

First, try small, simulated data sets to make
sure the model is correct and getting the right answers.
Then increase data set sizes.

Size itself shouldn't be a problem, but arithmetic issues
can be.  Stan doesn't do any kind of automatic ignoring
of illegal or missing values, and if you wind up with
arithmetic overflow/underflow in the wrong places, it will
just reject everything.

Why don't you think normal(0,1) priors are appropriate?
Are you expecting large values for the coefficients?

Are you sure your professor's approach in Stata got a sensible
answer?  If so, could you post the stata model or whatever
it was that was called to do this?

Your model in Stan could be made a lot faster by vectorizing
(and probably with some algebra), but you should first make sure
you're trying to fit the right model.

Are you sure that you don't have values that are overflowing
exp?  If you do arithmetic that winds up with not-a-number
values or infinite values, Stan will just reject the samples.
These can often be tamed with a little algebra.

What's the scale of the data?  That test for > 700
is worrisome, because exp(x)/(1 + exp(x)) is going to be 1
for values much less than 700 in floating point arithmetic!
This is very worrisome:

 >          if( zeta[i] > 700 )
 >              w[i] <- 1;
 >          else
 >              w[i] <- exp(zeta[i])/(1+exp(zeta[i]));

And then you use (1 - w[i]), and subtraction is notoriously
bad for arithmetic precision with values of w[i] close to 1
or close to 0.

- Bob

Sorry, should have reattached the model to the latest email! It's attached here. In this version I've put the desired quantity (log_mu) plus the interim ones not needed (beta1_stz & beta1_long) in transformed parameters. I'll stick with this for now, will see if it's still tenable in terms of memory when I get to the full implementation.

And what I meant by "prevents vectorization" was that I had to use a loop like

for (n in 1:N)
    log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));

instead of vector addition/multiplication like

log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;

Thanks again! Kyle

> > my only option is to also store the interim quantities by putting them all in the transformed parameters block. Is that
> > accurate? Not a big deal for this model, just keeping an eye towards my eventual model which is huge...
>
> Can you send a working model that perhaps saves too much
> and indicate which variables you want to save?  It's hard
> to tell from code fragments.
>
> You can (re)define whatever you want in generated quantities and
> it'll get saved.  The generated quantities are only computed
> once per iteration, not once per leapfrog step, and they're
> computed with double values rather than auto-dif variables for
> gradients, so they're much faster.  The problem is that it
> can require redundant definitions.
>
> For example, you can add this to generated quantities and log_mu
> will get saved:
>
>    generated quantities {
>      vector[N] log_mu;
>      for (n in 1:N)
>        log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));
>
> That is, assuming everything on the right side is either data, a parameter,
> or a transformed parameter.  If not, the values might be able to be
> recomputed.
>
> Loops involving only arithmetic on double values, like the above,
> are very fast in Stan.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] efficiency of stan and mcmc methods in general
messages.body_plain:
Hi, thank you very very much for your answer.

> Stan's not going to be super fast in its current
> incarnation for 1M data points, no matter what you do.
> So if you want a regression fit in 3 minutes for
> 1M data points and 120 parameters, you're probably going
> to have to look elsewhere.
>
> But if your model makes sense, Stan should be able to
> fit it, even with 1M data points.

I'm sorry if made it look like I was complaining with the software or anything like that, I sincerely admire how you guys made a pretty well organized and quick software in so little time. I'm more curious in fact, about how much time should I expect a model this big (1M x 120 parameters) to converge, or at least come close to that, using Stan and also using MCMC methods in general (Gibbs would probably takes a lot since the priors are not conjugate), this considering I'm using all the 8 cores of the processor to generate 1 chain each. A full day? Some hours? Less than one hour?

>
> I don't understand your model, but have some general
> advice.
>
> First, try small, simulated data sets to make
> sure the model is correct and getting the right answers.
> Then increase data set sizes.

I came to learn this by the worse way (not that bad, thought) some months ago, so my code posted is using simulated data.

>
> Size itself shouldn't be a problem, but arithmetic issues
> can be.  Stan doesn't do any kind of automatic ignoring
> of illegal or missing values, and if you wind up with
> arithmetic overflow/underflow in the wrong places, it will
> just reject everything.

That might be the problem that is making my model take too long to converge, I'll try to debug this.

>
> Why don't you think normal(0,1) priors are appropriate?
> Are you expecting large values for the coefficients?

I just think that it doesn't expose correctly my uncertainty about the parameters, 1e2 is as much credible, a priori, as 0 for a parameter value. For example, I got a lot of values in the range of those two numbers for my estimates in MLE.

>
> Are you sure your professor's approach in Stata got a sensible
> answer?  If so, could you post the stata model or whatever
> it was that was called to do this?

The results were pretty similar to those I got using R. I don't have the results of it right not with me, but it seens he just followed the syntax zip count child camper, inflate(persons) vuong in this <http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/stata/dae/zip.htm> tutorial (links work on this mailing list?).

It's seens that Stata uses an algorithm that fits the constant only model, and then the full model, this might be well optimized for the zero-inflated problem. And, also, my professor's version is multicore, if I'm not mistaken: so, these two reasons might explain why he got convergence so quickly.

>
> Your model in Stan could be made a lot faster by vectorizing
> (and probably with some algebra), but you should first make sure
> you're trying to fit the right model.

I read in some post in the mailing list that matrices are slower than loops, so, I assumed the same for vectors and wrote everything in term of loops. But vectors are better the arrays with loops? Or are you referring to another thing with the word "vectorizing"?

>
> Are you sure that you don't have values that are overflowing
> exp?  If you do arithmetic that winds up with not-a-number
> values or infinite values, Stan will just reject the samples.
> These can often be tamed with a little algebra.
>
> What's the scale of the data?  That test for > 700
> is worrisome, because exp(x)/(1 + exp(x)) is going to be 1
> for values much less than 700 in floating point arithmetic!
> This is very worrisome:
>
> >          if( zeta[i] > 700 )
> >              w[i] <- 1;
> >          else
> >              w[i] <- exp(zeta[i])/(1+exp(zeta[i]));

That's true, -log(.Machine$double.eps) in R gave me 36.04. I'm ashamed I forgot about this temporary "hack" I left there.

>
> And then you use (1 - w[i]), and subtraction is notoriously
> bad for arithmetic precision with values of w[i] close to 1
> or close to 0.

That's something I didn't payed attention, I'll correct that.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] assigning random effects to observations
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob, that's great! I guess I didn't understand "Stan allows local variables to be declared in blocks" (from the manual) - I was thinking about that in terms of loops, didn't think to extrapolate...

On Fri, Apr 5, 2013 at 10:45 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
>
> On 4/5/13 12:51 AM, Kyle Foreman wrote:
> > Sorry, should have reattached the model to the latest email! It's attached here. In this version I've put the desired
> > quantity (log_mu) plus the interim ones not needed (beta1_stz & beta1_long) in transformed parameters. I'll stick with
> > this for now, will see if it's still tenable in terms of memory when I get to the full implementation.
>
> Given that the variables you don't
> need to store show up only in the transformed parameters
> block, this is easy.  You just want to replace your:
>
>   transformed parameters {
>     vector[N] log_mu;       // need to store this
>     vector[S] beta1_stz;    // don't need to store this
>     vector[N] beta1_long;   // don't need to store this
>
>     beta1_stz <- beta1 - mean(beta1);
>     for (n in 1:N)
>         beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[state[n]];
>     log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;
>   }
>
> with this:
>
>   transformed parameters {
>     vector[N] log_mu;       // need to store this
>     {
>        vector[S] beta1_stz;    // don't need to store this
>        vector[N] beta1_long;   // don't need to store this
>
>        beta1_stz <- beta1 - mean(beta1);
>        for (n in 1:N)
>           beta1_long[n] <- beta1_stz[state[n]];
>        log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) + beta1_long;
>     }
> }
>
> That makes beta1_stz and beta1_long local variables, but exposes
> log_mu to the model.
>
>
> > And what I meant by "prevents vectorization" was that I had to use a loop like
> > |
> > for (n in 1:N)
> >      log_mu[n] <- log_pop[n] + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year[n]) + (beta1[state[n]] - mean(beta1));
> > |
> > instead of vector addition/multiplication like
> > |
> > log_mu <- log_pop + alpha0 + (alpha1 * year) +beta1_long;
>
> Looping, assignment and arithmetic are all compiled to C++,
> so they're much faster than in an interpreted language.
> In fact, the loop version can be faster because it doesn't
> do any intermediate allocations of vectors.
>
> Where you get a big boost from vectorization in Stan
> is where there's a reduction, such as a dot product, that takes

messages.subject: koyck model in stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi to everyone on the STAN users mailng list : I'll try to be brief but I wanted to explain the history of my problem first. The model I'm trying to fit is called the koyck disributed lag and has  a long classical history. In fact, it was developed in 1951
in the Ph.D thesis of Koyck. Phoebus dhrymes actually wrote a whole book on it and there have been many, many papers on it because estimating it, even classically, was not easy before computers got powerful. This is because there
are similarities between the koyck model and the GLS model ( serial correlation ) that are not necessary to go into here.

But I'm not so sure about it's history as far as bayesian attempts to estimate it. The paper that attempts to estimate it using gibbs sampling is attached but I found an error in it ( equation 44 ) and the authors don't provide the explicit GIbbs sampling
 code that estimated the model so I'm not so sure about the correctness of the results.  Also, there is definitely an issue at the boundary when rho is near 1 so that could be the reason why I have had so many problems estimating it. The beginning of attached  paper provides a discussion of the gelman-meng example and how one can get ridges in the likelihood or a bi-modal likelihood depending on the true parameter values.  The actual koyck model is discussed on pages 19-22. ( although the discussion between pages 12-18 is also quite relevant ) and pages 23-24 talked about problems at the boundary and how to deal with them.

My history with the model is that I worked on the bayesian estimation of it about 3 years ago. I made three different attempts:

1) I tried Rjags. ( I have that code if anyone is interested ).

2) I wrote my own code using gibbs sampling. When that didn't work, I wrote a metropolis hastings algoriithm. That wasn't successful either. ( I have that R code also ).

3) I tried to use the R admit package. That package generates a mixture of student t-densities as the proposal for an MH algorithm. It was actually the most successful of the three attempts but when the rho parameters was near the boundaty,
it also had problems.

The main problem is that the model I'm estimating with real data would be expected to have estimates of rho in the (0.9 - 1.0) range so having problems near the boundary is a real problem.

So, I heard about STAN a month or so ago and, after reading about HMC and NUTS, I finally tried it tonight. I didn't get good parameter estimates but of course I could be doing something incorrectly. I've only just started reading the Jags manual but this model is actually not that different from an AR(1) because a koyck distributed lag reduces to something pretty similar to an AR(1). So, the AR(1) model in the STAN manual really helped a lot.

>From reading the manual and Ben's great postings, it seems that RSTAN assumes flat improper priors for parameters that aren't explicity given a prior. So, I think the model matches what is in the paper as far as the joint prior.

Also,  I realize that it's a lot of work to look at the paper and the model etc but, if  anyone is interested, I'd really appreciate it and maybe something interesting could come out of it. I originally emailed Andrew a month or so ago about making a
contest on estimating this model on his blog but then he mentioned STAN which I had zero knowledge of.  Thanks Andrew.

As far as how my 3 years ago journey ended,  I ended up estimating the model using optimization methods but I'd love to know if it actually can be estimated using any kind of MCMC approach. Plus, when you use classical methods, you
have to decide on what time window to use to re-update the model estimates etc. A bayesian approach would avoid the need for that.

Or maybe it's a rare example of a model that just cannot be estimated using an MCMC approach. Thank you to anyone who wants to take a look. If anyone is interested, then my suggestion would be to read pages 1-22 of the attached paper. It's well written and really clear. It's only the Gibbs sampling results that I'm skeptical of. Thank you very much and if anyone has any questions about the model, feel free to ask me. Also, one more piece of info: 3 years back, I did get help from Ed Greenberg as far as asking him about my GIbbs sampling R code  and he wasn't able to figure out why my Gibbs sampling R code wasn't working so  I'm pretty certain that it's not possible to estimate it using regular GIbbs sampling.

Finally, my thanks to all of the people involved in Stan and Rstan. The instructions for getting it to run are so well written that it was a breeze. I always have bad times with software installations and, aside from my dopey locale problem, it was a piece of cake getting STAN and Rstan to work on my linux machine. Also, although I only started reading it today, the STAN manual is incredible with all the examples and details and explanations. and the users list is amazingly educational also. Thank you all  very much.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Mark

As an aside, if anyone knows anything that would help me understand NUTS more, please let me know. The authors, Andrew and Matt, are both well known and extremely clear in their writings but the connection between binary trees and their depth and using that information to decide when to stop the trajectory generation is something I'm just not getting.  Thanks again.

messages.subject: Re: koyck model in stan
messages.body_plain:
Mmmm, why don't you assign priors? I have just changed your code as follows,
data {
    int<lower=0> N; // number of data points
    real y[N];
    real x[N];
}

parameters {
    real <lower=0, upper=1> rho;
    real <lower=0> sigma;
    real beta;
}

transformed parameters{

    real <lower=0> sigmas;
    sigmas <- sqrt(sigma);
}

model {
    for ( n in 2:N)
        y[n] ~ normal(rho * y[n-1] + beta * (1-rho) * x[n], sigmas);

    // Priors
    rho ~ uniform(0,1);
    beta ~ normal(0,100);
    sigma ~ inv_gamma(2,1);
}

and it works good... :) Without that, I got totally non-sense...

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] is this paper at related to the No U-Turn concept in NUTS
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] is this paper at related to the No U-Turn concept in NUTS
messages.body_plain:
Nope, the two algorithms are fundamentally different on a variety of levels.  The paper you introduce is measuring curvature at various scales for classification, appeals to the Frenet-Serret formulas which are valid only in 2 and 3 dimensions, etc whereas NUTS is specific to Markov Chain Monte Carlo.  In particular, NUTS is a specific application of Neal's "ensemble MCMC" approach (http://arxiv.org/abs/1101.0387).

Here's what's going on.  What we want to be able to do is terminate trajectories when they "turn around", as any motion after the turning point reduces the distance between the initial point and the proposal, increases autocorrelations, and wastes computation.  Unfortunately we can't apply any termination criterion to a HMC trajectory without breaking detailed balance.  NUTS gets around this by introducing an intermediate ensemble, initial point -> binary tree -> proposal point, that preserves the target distribution.  If we use our previous termination criterion on every subtree within the intermediate binary tree, then the building of the tree terminates approximately at the turning point we desired above but without breaking detailed balance.

> Nope, the two algorithms are fundamentally different on a variety of levels.  The paper you introduce is measuring curvature at various scales for classification, appeals to the Frenet-Serret formulas which are valid only in 2 and 3 dimensions, etc whereas NUTS is specific to Markov Chain Monte Carlo.  In particular, NUTS is a specific application of Neal's "ensemble MCMC" approach (http://arxiv.org/abs/1101.0387).

NUTS gets around this by introducing an intermediate ensemble, initial point -> binary tree -> proposal point, that preserves the target distribution. I don't think anyone immediately grasps NUTS -- it certainly took me a loooooooong time to fully understand it.  I would recommend first making sure you understand how "windows" work in HMC (Radford discusses them in his HMC paper, but his ensemble paper goes into more depth).  With windows you have a transition initial point -> window -> proposed point that nicely parallels NUTS.   If you can prove that windows preserve the target distribution then it's pretty easy to show that a tree of specific depth (or a random depth) does so as well.

Once you have that, you'll need to convince yourself why a termination criterion on HMC breaks detailed balance (just keep reversing everything -- there's no reason why an arbitrary initial point would satisfy the termination criterion when simulating backwards from the final point).  Lastly, how does the binary tree get around this?  Admittedly, this is the hardest part.

If any of the individual steps trip you up let me know -- in order to convince myself I've written a bunch of scattered LaTeX notes that might be of help.

> On Saturday, April 6, 2013 2:24:16 AM UTC-4, Mark Leeds wrote:
> > From reading the manual and Ben's great postings, it seems that RSTAN assumes flat improper priors for parameters that aren't explicity given a prior. So, I think the model matches what is in the paper as far as the joint prior.
>
> Minor correction: The priors are uniform over their declared support, unless you bend the prior explicitly with a sampling statement in the model {} block such as beta ~ normal(0,1). But a uniform prior is proper if the support is bounded on both sides, which is the case here with rho in (0,1).
>
> As to your model, the wall time would improve if you pulled the sampling statement out of the loop:
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N; // number of data points
>   real y[N];
>   real x[N];
> }
>
> model {
>  real mu[N];
>  mu[0] <- y[0];
>  for ( n in 2:N)
>    mu[n] ~ rho * y[n-1] + beta * (1-rho) * x[n];
>
>  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> }
>
> If you are quite sure that in your real example that rho is large, then you can change the lower bound of the support to .8 or so, and it will sample a bit better because the unconstrained parameter underlying rho will be closer to symmetric. Also, like Carlos said, some reasonable but weak priors would help too.
>
> Ben
>
>

> }

>  real mu[N];

>
>  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> }
> generated quantities {
>   real beta;
>   beta <- beta1mrho / (1 - rho)
> }
>
> That might get you better geometry.
>
> Ben

On 4/6/13 7:41 PM, Marco wrote:
>
>>
>> I think the sum of an array and the sum of a vector are essentially the same in terms of speed. Either way, sum()
>> accumulates the derivatives in an efficient manner.

Exactly.

> Do you know if sum() takes care of float precision using, for example, Kahan summation algorithm? My code now is highly
> dependent on something like that.

No, it doesn't.  It's just a straight-up sum.
It does the gradients independently, so those
will be OK even if some of the terms in the sum
underflow.

But are you sure you need something like Kahan summation?
It should only be necessary to add numbers of very
different orders of magnitude, and then is only going
to help when you have many of the smaller numbers that
can eventually add up to something that makes a difference
on the larger scale.

You can always code it up yourself in the Stan program
and see if it makes a difference:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahan_summation_algorithm

Warning:  it will be much slower because of all the
extra work for derivatives (time is roughly proportional
to the size of expression built up for the log
probability).

We could do this more efficiently by implementing
kahan_sum() and pairwise_sum() functions:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pairwise_summation

I'll put it on the to-do list.

- Bob

It depends how complicated the log probability
function is.  It all comes down to the number of
function applications in computing it.  Each of
those functions needs to have its partial derivative
calculated and the chain rule applied, which is where
all the time goes.

To get a feeling, simulate smaller data sets, then increase
the size to measure the trend.

I could fit 1M data point IRT models with 20K parameters
in hours with four chains.

Do you really have 8 cores, or is it hyperthreading?  It's
often faster not to use the hyperthreading from Intel.

- Bob

> optimized for the zero-inflated problem. And, also, my professor's version is multicore, if I'm not mistaken: so, these
> two reasons might explain why he got convergence so quickly.

OK -- if you have values you trust, you can try
initializing the Stan model with those values and see
what happens.  That will at least help you diagnose whether
it's a convergence issue.  But having said that, maximum
likelihood (or MAP) estimates can be far away from the
majority of the posterior probability mass in some examples.

Multicore only does so much.  It'll be at most
N times faster where N is the number of corese.

>> Your model in Stan could be made a lot faster by vectorizing
>> (and probably with some algebra), but you should first make sure
>> you're trying to fit the right model.
> I read in some post in the mailing list that matrices are slower than loops, so, I assumed the same for vectors and
> wrote everything in term of loops. But vectors are better the arrays with loops? Or are you referring to another thing
> with the word "vectorizing"?

???

An array of vectors is faster at pulling out the vectors.

Otherwise, use as many matrix operations as you can.  Some
don't help much for speed, but none of them are slower than
looping.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: koyck model in stan
messages.body_plain:
Here are some initial comments/results concerning Bob's koyck model:

1) Unfortunately, the koyck model in the wiki is incorrect. They just wrote down the reduced form but in that reduced form, there should be a (1-lambda) multiplying beta. There are
two different versions  of the reduced form of the koyck distributed model but neither of them are the one in the wiki. The two forms result from the particular assumption put on the
initial error term in the long form. I generally refer to them ( in my lingo ) as the depooter model and the baltagi model ( without intercepts )

1) depooter model ( one from earlier attachment on page 19 of adl_gibbs ):   y_t = lambda* y_t-1 + beta(1-lambda)*X_t + epsilon_t ( replacing rho in the paper with lambda )

2) baltagi ( 6.10 on page 136 of attached ) : y_t = lambda*y_t-1 + beta*(1-lambda)*X_t + epsilon_t - lambda*epsilon_t-1

I tend to work with depooter's  but I've also estimated 2) using numerical optimization in R.

Even though the wiki model doesn't match 1) or 2), I played with Bob's model in the following ways:

A) first I took alpha out and this had no negative effects. The estimates remained fine regardless of the value of lambda.

B) then I went ahead and took the model in A) and added the (1-lambda) term to the X_t term in order to make it the depooter model. This is where problems occur.  When
lambda is in the higher range, 0.7-0.95, the estimates of beta get worse as lambda gets closer to 1.0. This is because, the coefficient (1-lambda)*beta becomes less
indentifiable as lambda gets closer to 1.0 ( this is what is discussed in adl_gibbs.pdf on pages 23-24 ).  So, atleast now I know that the problem is due to the fact that lambda is involved
in both coefficients. I haven't tried centering yet  and that will be next effort but I have one sort of related question before I work on that.

In the classical formulation, ( where I estimate the model numerical using gradients or linear regression ), then if I estimated the Depooter model using Bob's original formulation
and then just divided the model beta estimate, namely beta hat,  by (1-lambda hat) to get a betastar hat, that's a legitimate "trick" to avoid dealing with the parameter being involved in both
coefficients. Bit this is only a valid "trick" when estimating it classically I think.

In the bayesian setting, that's cheating right, because the original model isn't being told that there's a (1-lambda) term on the beta being estimated in the original model ?
I just  want to make sure that doing that is illegal statistically in the bayesian formulation.  If it's legal, then I can use Bob's formulation to back out the value of beta hat
in my formulation. But that would seem illegal to me because one is making an assumption about the coeffs of the model and not telling  the model about that assumption during estimation ?
Anyway, I'm going to try that next and see what happens: Estimate the model using Bob's formulation but back out the estimate implied by my formulation and see if it's correct ?

Assuming that I'm correct about that being cheating, my next step after that will be centering. The Stan code and R code for the Depooter model without alpha is provided below.
I tried different "triplets of estimates" , using the same near 1.0 value of lambda each time and lowering it away from 1.0 using the next triplet to see when good estimates of beta  start to occur.
Thanks for any insights regarding my cheating question.

R CODE
#==========================================================================================================

library("rstan");

T <- 200;
x <- rnorm(T,0,1);

#=========================================
# NOT OKAY
#=========================================
#beta <- 1.0;
#lambda <- 0.95
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 2.6;
#lambda <- 0.95
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 0.5;
#lambda <- 0.95
#sigma <- 1.0
#====================================
# NOT OKAY
#====================================
#beta <- 1.0;
#lambda <- 0.90
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 2.6;
#lambda <- 0.90
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 0.5;
#lambda <- 0.90
#sigma <- 1.0
#========================================
#NOT OKAY
#=========================================
#beta <- 1.0;
#lambda <- 0.85
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 2.6;
#lambda <- 0.85
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 0.5;
#lambda <- 0.85
#sigma <- 1.0
#====================================
# NOT OKAY
#====================================
#beta <- 1.0;
#lambda <- 0.80
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 2.6;
#lambda <- 0.80
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 0.5;
#lambda <- 0.80
#sigma <- 1.0
#====================================
# NOT OKAY
#====================================
#beta <- 1.0;
#lambda <- 0.75
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 2.6;
#lambda <- 0.75
#sigma <- 1.0

#beta <- 0.5;
#lambda <- 0.75
#sigma <- 1.0
#====================================
# ALMOST OKAY
#====================================
# OKAY
#beta <- 1.0;
#lambda <- 0.70
#sigma <- 1.0

# OKAY
#beta <- 2.6;
#lambda <- 0.70
#sigma <- 1.0

# STILL NOT OKAY
#beta <- 0.5;
#lambda <- 0.70
#sigma <- 1.0
#=============================================
# BETTER BUT NOT QUITE
#beta <- 0.5;
#lambda <- 0.65
#sigma <- 1.0
#=============================================
# OKAY !!!!!!
beta <- 0.5;
lambda <- 0.60
sigma <- 1.0
#===========================================
y <- rep(NA,T);

y[1] <- rnorm(1,beta * (1 - lambda) * x[1],sigma);

for (t in 2:T)

  y[t] <- rnorm(1, beta * (1 - lambda) * x[t] + lambda * y[t-1], sigma);

fit <- stan(file="koyck_nalpha_oneminus.stan", data=c("T","y","x"), iter=1000, chains=4);
print(fit)

#===========================================================================================================
# STAN CODE
#===========================================================================================================

data {
  int<lower=0> T; // number of time points
  real y[T]; // output at time t
  real x[T]; // predictor for time t
}
parameters {

  real beta; // slope
  real <lower=0, upper=1> lambda; // lag
  real <lower=0> sigma; // noise scale
}
model {

  beta ~ cauchy(0,5);

  lambda ~ uniform(0,1);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
  for (t in 2:T)

    y[t] ~ normal((1-lambda) * beta * x[t] + lambda * y[t-1],sigma);

}

messages.body_plain:
Many of these time-series models assume that the
outputs are centered so that there's no intercept term.

Just think of basic regression.  If you have

    y[n] = alpha + beta * x[n] + epsilon[n]

and

    epsilon[n] ~ normal(0,sigma)

then if alpha is estimated as non-zero, then the slope-only
model is going to be less effective,

   y[n] = beta2 * x[n] + epsilon2[n]

and the slope beta2 won't match the original slope beta
because it needs to try to take up some of the work
formerly done by alpha.  And the scale of the error
distribution for epsilon2 will be larger.

Now if you take y[n] and subtract the average value
(which is going to be alpha = mean(y) in a basic linear regression),

   y2[n] <- y[n] - mean(y);

then the regression

   y2[n] = beta * x[n] + epsilon[n];

I don't know what a good reference is for centering.  It should
be discussed heavily within all these time series models because
they do it all the time.

There's a bit of discussion of completely standardizing
(y -> (y - mean(y))/sd(y)), which both centers and rescales.

- Bob

> sampleSize<-1e5
> bbgg <- c(rep(1,sampleSize/4),rep(0,sampleSize/4),rep(2,sampleSize/2))
> for(i in 1:3)
> {

> x2 <-

> c(rnorm(sampleSize/4,i*1.1**1000*,runif(1,1,5)),rnorm(sampleSize/4,i*1.4**1000*,runif(1,1,5)),rnorm(sampleSize/2,i*1.7**1000*,runif(1,1,5)))
> bbgg <- cbind(bbgg,x1,x2)
> }

Can you remind me what these variables are?  Is it just
a matter of one set of regression-like coefficients being scaled
to 1000 times the others?  This is a HUGE difference on
a transformed scale like the logistic if that's an issue
(I can't recall the details of your model, I'm afraid).

Do you change priors in the model, too?  Change of data scale
for predictors should be accompanied by an inverse change
of scale on the priors.  Making predictors 1000 times as big
means coefficients are 1/1000 times as big.

> Placing print(lp__) right before the end of model section shows that Stan is actively calculating log-likelihoods of my
> model although it doesn't move to the next iteration. In fact, the log-likelihood seems to be moving in a circular way.
>
> I know almost nothing about how HMC and NUTS work, so I don't have a good idea of why covariates with different
> magnitudes are making the Stan unable to continue. Do you know some work around for this problem?

Regularizing the predictors usually helps :-)

Regression with hugely varying coefficients and floating
point arithmetic don't mix well.

Have you tried init=0 option?  That may give you a more stable
place from which to start.  We don't have a user controllable
option for scale of initialization noise, and with big
regressions, it can cause problems.

We've been playing around a bit with adaptation, but the
problem with getting stuck early on is that Stan's probably
working very hard to find scales for the proposals that
can let it move.

If it calculates log likelihoods and then the params don't
move, it's because the proposals are getting rejected, which
is probably due to step sizes being too large.  You could try
manually setting lower step sizes until you find one that works.
You shouldn't need to tune number of steps -- NUTS will handle
that.

- Bob

> Thanks Andrew, Bob and Ben for your comments. Going forward, I will refer to bob's formulation as the "wiki" koyck and
> the formulation with rho on both coefficients as the "depooter" koyck. I don't think
> we need to deal with the baltagi version. It only differs from the depooter in the initial assumption about the error
> term on the long infinite coefficient formulation.

Overall, the model won't make sense in a Bayesian setting with the
parameterization (1-lambda)* beta * x[n].  The problem is that
beta needs to get huge when lambda gets close to 1, so what kind
of prior makes sense for it?

Putting a prior on beta makes much more sense.

> A) Ben:  I will try the "backing out" of betahat method using bob's formulation and see how that goes. Note though that
> the short form of the model in the wiki is incorrect because there is no transformation that
> will take you from the infinite coefficient formulation at the top of the wiki to the reduced form that they have in the
> wiki. I think the code you sent  is related or the same as the backing out method. I have to look
> at it more carefully. I'm just not so convinced it's valid to do that in the bayesian setting because rho being involved
> in the X_t coefficient, should effect the joint posterior. But I'll worry about understanding
> that later.

The issue is that you're sampling here.  You can transform samples
and still get valid samples.

For example,

    y ~ normal(0,1);
    z <- y * sigma + mu;

z will have a normal(mu,sigma) distribution in the samples.

You can't do it the other way around
without accounting for the Jacobian.  For instance, this
won't do what you expect in tems of samples for y.

   z <- (y - mu) / sigma;
   z ~ normal(0,1);

For this, you need to adjust for the Jacobian because the
variable being sampled (on the left of the ~) is transformed.
(It is kosher if sigma is a constant rather than another parameter,
because the log Jacobian determinant is log |1/sigma|, which is
still constant if sigma is a constant.)

In Stan, that adjustment is the following (assuming sigma is
constrained to be positive):

    lp__ <- lp__ - log(sigma);

> B) Andrew: Thanks for the ARM centering reference and paper recommendation. I will read the relevant pages in gelman and

Most of the time series I've seen assume centered data.  But
this may be a coincidence due to what people have sent me and
what I've read in the Wikipedia.

For instance, in the paper someone else referred me to by
Kim, Shepherd and Chib on stochastic volatility and GARCH
models:

   http://finance.martinsewell.com/stylized-facts/volatility/KimShephardChib1998.pdf

They call it "mean corrected return", but it's the same idea.
It's characterized by the lack of an intercept term in the regression.

Most descriptions of Gaussian process models assume centered data (such
as most of the discussion in the Rasmussen and Williams book).

:the real koyck distributed lag model is actually the long form with the infinite sum. the koyck transformation reduces it to the simpler form with the beta*(1-lambda). So, it has to be valid ( maybe not in the bayesian sense ) econometrically speaking because the koyck distributed lag is actually

A)  y_t = beta * (sum from i = 1 to infinity of lamba^i X_t-i ) + e_t So, a beta coefficient times an infinite sum of past coefficients each with coefficient_i equal to lambda to the i.

The reduced form of the koyck model  above is

B) y_t = lambda*y_t-1 + beta*(1-lambda)*X_t.  + v_t ( v_t normal assuming v_t = e_t - lambda e_t-1 )

B) is just the transform of A) using the koyck transformation. You can see the baltagi pdf or adl_gibbs.pdf for how one gets from the long form to the shorter form.  So, it is valid
econometrically. Now the adl_gibbs.pdf paper claims that the model above can be estimated using gibbs sampling. It talks somewhat separately about problems at the boundary and the
gelman-meng paper involving bimodal posteriors and posteriors with ridges etc.

You're understanding of STAN and bayesian is way greater than mine so you may be interested in reading pages 1-23 of adl_gibbs.pdf.

The first 10 or so pages talk about gibbs sampling and about possible problems at the boundary and  also the gelman-meng paper involving bimodal posteriors and posteriors with ridges etc.

Then the next 10 pages or talk about various regression models and how they can be estimated using gibbs sampling. The last model ( 19-22) is the koyck distributed lag I describe above.
They claim that the model can be ( and is ) estimated using gibbs sampling. They get very nice conditional densities and claim to sample from them to estimate
the model. This I doubt because I tried it.

But then, on pages 22-23, they kind of wave their hands and do talk about the identifiability issue when rho is near 1 and how special priors for rho might be able to take care of it etc.  This part is a little
unclear to me and you may be able to understand it a lot better. and it may be possible to implement in STAN ?

So, overall the paper is kind of a little unclear because they claim to estimate the model using gibbs sampling but then in the next breath, they talk about how rho near
1 causes problems. I think the paper was published somewhere ( there's also an error in equation 44. this could have contributed to gibbs sampling working possibly ? ) but like I said,
I doubt the results are correct. On the other hand, if we could understand the "special prior" they recommend using in order to deal with the boundary issue, then maybe it is possible  using STAN?

> > term on the long infinite coefficient formulation.

> parameterization (1-lambda)* beta * x[n].  The problem is that
> beta needs to get huge when lambda gets close to 1, so what kind
> of prior makes sense for it?
>
> Putting a prior on beta makes much more sense.

I think it is actually the opposite: when the autoregressive parameter (lambda) gets close to 1, beta needs to go to zero. Technically, beta isn't identified by the data in that case, but presumably you want the prior to be such that the posterior distribution of beta is near zero so that you conclude the outcome is a random walk.

So, you could specify a normal or t prior on beta where the prior location is zero and the prior scale depends multiplicatively 1 - lambda^2. But I still think it is better to parameterize the coefficient on x as beta1mlambda, which stands for beta * (1 - lambda), again with a normal or t prior on beta1mlambda where the prior location is zero and the prior scale depends multiplicatively 1 - lambda^2. Then make beta a generated quantity.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob: I don't want to comment on beta_raw because beta_raw is from a model that can't be deduced from the original koyck model. ( the long form where there are an infinite number of coefficients ).
The model in the wiki is not possible in the sense of being a model that can be obtained from a transformation of the original infinite sum formulation. That's important because the whole point of obtaining
the reduced form of koyck distributed lag is to be able to estimate the parameters in THE ORIGINAL LONG FORM OF THE MODEL. In other words, the long form is a model that captures dampening behavior where the weights of the coefficients get less and less weight the further you go back in time. But estimating that model is difficult directly. So, the koyck transformation results in the "short form" that is
much easier to estimate ( atleast classically. but you can run into problems there too if you don't use numerical optimization and gradients ).  The point I'm trying to make is that the short form of model in the wiki doesn't have a long form correspondence. It's incorrect in terms of it corresponding to anything useful from a "distributed lag" viewpoint.  Wiki's can definitely be wrong. I've seen this happen before.

So, getting back to "Depooter" koyck:

The simplistic way I see it is that   lambda going to one in the "depooter" koyck causes an "indentifiability" problem because beta*(1-lambda) gets close to zero so it's impossible to estimate beta.

but let me write here what Lennart wrote to me in an email.  I don't have a hardcopy of the email so I'll just write it. and Lennart definitely knows what he's doing so I would bet there's some validity to the following:

Quoting Lennart from May 16, 2010 in an email to Mark Leeds:

" Hi Mark: I read your email and the relevant pages in the paper by Depooter et al: I think it is the prior that causes the problems. Indeed there must be a ridge in the likelihood for rho equal to 1 which I think is
not integrable ( having integral of infinity ),  if the prior does not "correct" it. So, under the uniform prior for rho,  the posterior kernel does not correspond to a proper distribution. In other words, intuitively
stated, the "scaling  constant" should be infinity which ruins the results.

I think a regularization prior for rho such as probability(rho) ~ (1-rho hat)^2 which keeps rho somewhat away from 1, ( similar to equation (52) in Depooter et al ) would solve the problems.".

End of Quote from Lennart Hoogerheide.

I can't remember what happened after this in terms of whether I tried this with the Admit package or not. I don't think I did because I didn't understand how that could be a prior because I thought
the prior needed to integrate to 1. At that point, I think I decided to give up and go the classical route using numerical optimization and gradients.

Anyway, maybe above sheds some light on the issue. It's pretty similar to what's talked about on pages 22-23 of adl_gibbs.pdf.

Ben: I'll read your email tomorrow. It's late and my brain hurts.

> much easier to estimate ( atleast classically. but you can run into problems there too if you don't use numerical

For maximum likelihood, there shouldn't be an issue until
lambda gets so close to 1 that beta overflows to keep up.

> long form correspondence. It's incorrect in terms of it corresponding to anything useful from a "distributed lag"

I'm just commenting on the Stan formulation and the
behavior you can expect from different parameterizations
of your model.

the Wikipedia entry!

> because beta*(1-lambda) gets close to zero so it's impossible to estimate beta.

Why does this make it impossible to estimate beta?
If there's an effect for the predictor, then beta should
just grow to compensate.

A Bayesian prior on beta (such as beta ~ normal(0,1000))
will stop beta from growing enough, so the
beta * (1 - rho) term will just go to zero as
lambda goes to 1.

:-)  I thought you wanted rho to go to 1 if the data
supported it.  If you really want to impose a strong enough
prior to bound rho away from 1, that will manage the scale

> End of Quote from Lennart Hoogerheide.

> I can't remember what happened after this in terms of whether I tried this with the Admit package or not. I don't think

The integral just needs to be finite, which is equivalent to
integrating to 1, but dropping the proportionality constant.
In this case it's easy because rho is constrained to [0,1].

> Anyway, maybe above sheds some light on the issue. It's pretty similar to what's talked about on pages 22-23 of

I think after you read Ben's mail you'll see we're all on
the same page again.  Ben also had some suggestions on the
non-independence of the prior on rho and beta.   You could
also overcome the issue that way, where the scale of beta is
allowed to grow as rho approaches 1.

> > koyck model. ( the long form where there are an infinite number of coefficients ).
>
> It's just a reparameterization of what you had, which
> will help with arithmetic stability in the estimate.
>
> Given what you say below, it shouldn't be necessary.
>
> > The model in the wiki is not possible in the sense of being a model that can be obtained from a transformation of the
> > original infinite sum formulation. That's important because the whole point of obtaining
> > the reduced form of koyck distributed lag is to be able to estimate the parameters in THE ORIGINAL LONG FORM OF THE
> > MODEL. In other words, the long form is a model that captures dampening behavior where the weights of the coefficients
> > get less and less weight the further you go back in time. But estimating that model is difficult directly. So, the koyck
> > transformation results in the "short form" that is
> > much easier to estimate ( atleast classically. but you can run into problems there too if you don't use numerical
> > optimization and gradients ).
>
> For maximum likelihood, there shouldn't be an issue until
> lambda gets so close to 1 that beta overflows to keep up.
>
> > The point I'm trying to make is that the short form of model in the wiki doesn't have a
> > long form correspondence. It's incorrect in terms of it corresponding to anything useful from a "distributed lag"
> > viewpoint.
>
> I'm not even sure what people use these models for!
> I'm just commenting on the Stan formulation and the
> behavior you can expect from different parameterizations
> of your model.
>
>  > Wiki's can definitely be wrong. I've seen this happen before.
>
> Of course --- that's why I was suggesting changing
> the Wikipedia entry!
>
> > So, getting back to "Depooter" koyck:
> >
> > The simplistic way I see it is that   lambda going to one in the "depooter" koyck causes an "indentifiability" problem
> > because beta*(1-lambda) gets close to zero so it's impossible to estimate beta.
>
> Why does this make it impossible to estimate beta?
> If there's an effect for the predictor, then beta should
> just grow to compensate.
>
> A Bayesian prior on beta (such as beta ~ normal(0,1000))
> will stop beta from growing enough, so the
> beta * (1 - rho) term will just go to zero as
> lambda goes to 1.
>
> > but let me write here what Lennart wrote to me in an email.  I don't have a hardcopy of the email so I'll just write it.
> > and Lennart definitely knows what he's doing so I would bet there's some validity to the following:
> >
> > Quoting Lennart from May 16, 2010 in an email to Mark Leeds:
> >
> > " Hi Mark: I read your email and the relevant pages in the paper by Depooter et al: I think it is the prior that causes
> > the problems. Indeed there must be a ridge in the likelihood for rho equal to 1 which I think is
> > not integrable ( having integral of infinity ),  if the prior does not "correct" it. So, under the uniform prior for
> > rho,  the posterior kernel does not correspond to a proper distribution. In other words, intuitively
> > stated, the "scaling  constant" should be infinity which ruins the results.
>
> > I think a regularization prior for rho such as probability(rho) ~ (1-rho hat)^2 which keeps rho somewhat away from 1, (
> > similar to equation (52) in Depooter et al ) would solve the problems.".
>
> :-)  I thought you wanted rho to go to 1 if the data
> supported it.  If you really want to impose a strong enough
> prior to bound rho away from 1, that will manage the scale
> of beta (to the degree that rho is bound away from 1).
>
> > End of Quote from Lennart Hoogerheide.
> >
> > I can't remember what happened after this in terms of whether I tried this with the Admit package or not. I don't think
> > I did because I didn't understand how that could be a prior because I thought
> > the prior needed to integrate to 1.
>
> The integral just needs to be finite, which is equivalent to
> integrating to 1, but dropping the proportionality constant.
> In this case it's easy because rho is constrained to [0,1].
>
> > At that point, I think I decided to give up and go the classical route using
> > numerical optimization and gradients.
> >
> > Anyway, maybe above sheds some light on the issue. It's pretty similar to what's talked about on pages 22-23 of
> > adl_gibbs.pdf.
> >
> > Ben: I'll read your email tomorrow. It's late and my brain hurts.
>
> I think after you read Ben's mail you'll see we're all on
> the same page again.  Ben also had some suggestions on the
> non-independence of the prior on rho and beta.   You could
> also overcome the issue that way, where the scale of beta is
> allowed to grow as rho approaches 1.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: calculation of Poisson log-likelihood from STAN does match dpois in R
messages.body_snippet:
Hi all

The calculation of the Poisson log-likelihood at each iteration in STAN differs from the dpois function in R.  Presumably there is a straightforward explanation to this that I've just missed?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] calculation of Poisson log-likelihood from STAN does match dpois in R
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] calculation of Poisson log-likelihood from STAN does match dpois in R
messages.body_plain:
One thing is that Stan automatically drops constants when they're not
needed for estimation.  E.G., the sqrt(2*pi) term in a normal
distribution is not included in the lp__.  This should be easy to
check, as the difference between dpois and lp__ should be a constant.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Wed, Apr 10, 2013 at 4:21 PM, atzap <ata...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi all
>
> The calculation of the Poisson log-likelihood at each iteration in STAN
> differs from the dpois function in R.  Presumably there is a straightforward
> explanation to this that I've just missed?  I note that the difference isn't
> constant if you plot out the two sets of estimates.
>
> Consider the follow model:
>
> m1p1 <- "
> data {
>  int<lower=0> y[50];
> }
> parameters {
>  real<lower = 0> lambda;
> }
> model {
>  lp__ <- lp__ + poisson_log(y,lambda);
> }"
>
>
> # Generate some data and initial values:
>
> data <- list(y =rpois(50, 100))
> init <- function(x){list(list("lambda" = runif(1)))}
>
>
> # And run a quick test:
>
> tmp1 <- stan(model_code = m1p1, data = data, pars = "lambda",
> init = init(), iter = 200, warmup = 100, thin = 1, chains = 1)
>
>
> # Extract the lambda estimates
>
> estlam <- extract(tmp1, "lambda")[[1]]
>
>
> # Plug them into dpois
>
> sapply(estlam, function(x){sum(dpois(x = data$y, lambda = x, log = T))})
>
>
> # Extract the STAN lp__ estimates
> # they should differ from the above line
>
> extract(tmp1, "lp__")[[1]]
>
>
>
> Many thanks,
> Andrew
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
HMC only requires log probability functions up
to an additive constant.  So Stan automatically drops
all terms in the log probability sum that involve only
constants.

Because

   log Poisson(y|lambda)
     = - y * log(lambda)
       - log y!
       - lambda

and you call it with y constant (declared as data),
the second term (- log gamma(y+1)) gets dropped.

- Bob

> lambda <- 100

[1] 4.60517
> log(lambda)
[1] 4.60517

On 4/10/13 11:15 PM, Marco wrote:
...

>> Do you change priors in the model, too?  Change of data scale
>> for predictors should be accompanied by an inverse change
>> of scale on the priors.
> Do I need to rescale an improper uniform prior too in this situation? Sorry for the n00b question, but I heard that I
> should consider a Jacobian here somehow depending on the rescale operation.

You only need to adjust the Jacobian for parameters,
not for data.

Rescaling predictors in a regression will affect the behavior
of the prior on the regression coefficients. But if it's
improper uniform, there's no effect.  Rescaling by a constant
wont' affect the uniform probabilty.

In general, rescaling itself doesn't need a Jacobian:

     log |d/dx  c * theta| = |c|

which is a constant, so can be dropped from the calculation
in Stan.

>> Regularizing the predictors usually helps :-)
> yeeh! It's working pretty well and fast now that I divided all my database columns by their standard deviation.

Andrew will be happy to hear it, because it's his
standard operating procedure advice.

>> Regression with hugely varying coefficients and floating
>> point arithmetic don't mix well.
> You mean I could lose precision, have unreliable results and/or would this affect stan's convergence?

You lose precision, which makes everything harder to do.
It will affect convergence if it's small, and lead to not
being able to do estimation at all if the variation is too large.

- Bob

B) I ran a similar scenario set to what I ran earlier in terms of sets of triplets of parameters ( each triplet only varies in beta values )  and then as I go down, I keep decreasing lambda to see how that effects
the beta estimates.

C) The results are better. The estimates of beta don't get totally whacky like they did in the earlier experiment but for lambda ( which of course used to be rho. we just changed notation somewhere along the way ) above 0.9, the beta estimates are still not very good. I put the beta estimate at the top of each triplet and gave it a "review" so that it's not necessary to re-run all the code. I set.seed(123) at the top
if the code before running each scenario but there's some randomness of course going on in STAN so the results won't be the same. It seems that below lambda = 0.9, the estimates pretty much
remain as good as they're going to get for the most part. In my other run where I explicitly code lambda(1-rho), the improvement seemed to be less spikey and more gradual. Not sure if that means
anything.

D) I don't claim to be an HMC expert but I'm trying to think about something that my understanding is not 100 percent clear on so hear me out if you don't mind. Lennart says that the log posterior goes to
infinity as rho goes to 1. I'm not clear on how he knows that but, assuming it's true: could the problem then correspond to the example on pages 30-31 of "Probabilistic Inference Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo
Methods" by Radford Neal. If someone could take a look at that discussion and the picture in c). The density is spiking up in one place and the values of A in that place are all very low so MCMC sampling will
be problematic. I don''t know enough about HMC ( atleast yet. as time permits, I'm going back over then DUANE paper for the 38th time ) yet to say anything with confidence but maybe the problem has something to do with that which I think is what Lennart was saying ?

1) restrict rho to be uniform(0,0.95). only problem with that is you leave out cases where rho really is greater than that.

2) use the prior that lennart suggested to force the posterior density to be zero when rho gets near 1.0.

posterior density is involved in HMC. I think it's only involved because it's the gradient of the posterior that's in the differential equations that simulate states of parameters. but if that's the case,  that's so different from regular metropolis where the actual posterior atleast gets plugged into on the top and bottom in the acceptance step. The metropolis argument makes perfect sense to me.  In HMC, the metrpolis type
acceptance is used  the actual posterior isn't even involved in the acceptance step !!!!!! and this continues to confuse me in terms of how one can just use multivariate normals ( I understand that the normals are conditional but that the conditionals are just the marginals because of independence of the two energies in the expression for the hamiltonian. I just don't understand why one don't plug into the posterior
like would be done in a regular metropolis step. that has something to do with sampling from the differential equations rather than from the density itself but I'm working on it  )  but I'm getting it slowly.
