> Methods" by Radford Neal. If someone could take a look at that discussion and the picture in c). The density is spiking up in one place and the values of A in that place are all very low so MCMC sampling will
> be problematic. I don''t know enough about HMC ( atleast yet. as time permits, I'm going back over then DUANE paper for the 38th time ) yet to say anything with confidence but maybe the problem has something to do with that which I think is what Lennart was saying ?

It sounds like you're dramatically over-thinking HMC, so let me try to explain.

In HMC you're not sampling from your target distribution pi(q), but rather an extended distribution pi(p, q) = pi(p | q) p (q).  Hamiltonian dynamics provides a Metropolis proposal for {p, q} which is accepted with the usual Metropolis acceptance procedure for the extended distribution pi(p, q).

You then get a sample from pi(q) by simply ignoring the variables p since the marginal of the extended distribution is the target distribution, \int dp pi(p, q) = pi(q) \int dp pi(p | q) = pi(q).

I haven't looked at your model in any depth, but if there is finite posterior density at rho = 1 then there will be problems sampling with HMC.  The problem is that when we transform rho to an unconstrained space the boundaries go to infinity, [0, 1] -> [-inf, inf].  If the posterior density is finite at rho = 1 then it will also be finite at rho_unconstrained = inf, and Hamiltonian dynamics falls apart when the Hamiltonian is non-zero at infinity.  Computationally it's easy to see why -- if the density is non-zero out there, then the chain needs to travel all the way out to infinity which would take an infinite amount of time, not to mention wreaking havoc on any numerical implementation.  This is case where using bouncing to constrain variables can help, but we haven't implemented that in Stan.

-Mike

messages.body_plain:
This isn't a bug in Stan.  But it does point out a number
of subtleties in the way Stan behaves w.r.t. constants
and (implicit) Jacobians.

I've updated the manual to try to make it clearer
what's going on.  I'll summarize here, with R code
to validate vs. Stan 1.2.

First, if y is a data variable and lambda a parameter variable,
when you write

    y ~ poisson(lambda);

Stan drops the normalizing term for y (because we only
need the log probability up to an additive constant that
doesn't depend on the params).

On the other hand,

    lp__ <- lp__ + poisson_log(y,lambda);

does NOT drop the normalizing terms.  So the difference
between these expressions of the model is that the
-log(y!) term is not added to lp__ in the sampling version.

This difference does NOT affect the samples that are drawn,
because it's only an additive term.

Second, if the declaration of lambda is constrained (as it
should be here),

   parameters {
     real<lower=0> lambda;
   }

then there's an additional term in the log probability corresponding
to the log derivative of the inverse transform.  We log transform,
so we actually run HMC/NUTS over y, where

    y = log(lambda).

The inverse transform is exp, so the log Jacobian is just

    log | d/dx exp(y) | =  y

                        = log(lambda)

What I got wrong before was thinking that the log Jacobian
was just lambda.  It's just y, which is log(lambda).  Daniel Lee worked
it out and set me straight (thanks!).

Here's an example in R, using Stan 1.2, that verifies everything's
working correctly  (I simplified to a single sample -- the issue's
the same with more than one sampling statement.)

poisson.stan
------------
parameters {
   real<lower=0> lambda;
}
model {
   3 ~ poisson(lambda);
}

Here's an R program to test the behavior,

poisson.R
---------
fit <- stan('poisson.stan',iter=100,chains=1);
fit_ss <- extract(fit);
fit_lambda <- fit_ss$lambda;
fit_lp <- fit_ss$lp__;

lpfun <- function(lam) { dpois(3,lam,log=TRUE) + log(lam) };
print("lambda, lp__, log_prob_from_R, diff")
for (n in 1:10) {
   print(paste(c(fit_lambda[n],
                 fit_lp[n],
                 lpfun(fit_lambda[n]),
                 fit_lp[n] - lpfun(fit_lambda[n]))));
}

> > D) I don't claim to be an HMC expert but I'm trying to think about something that my understanding is not 100 percent clear on so hear me out if you don't mind. Lennart says that the log posterior goes to
> > infinity as rho goes to 1. I'm not clear on how he knows that but, assuming it's true: could the problem then correspond to the example on pages 30-31 of "Probabilistic Inference Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo
> > Methods" by Radford Neal. If someone could take a look at that discussion and the picture in c). The density is spiking up in one place and the values of A in that place are all very low so MCMC sampling will

>
> It sounds like you're dramatically over-thinking HMC, so let me try to explain.
>
> In HMC you're not sampling from your target distribution pi(q), but rather an extended distribution pi(p, q) = pi(p | q) p (q).  Hamiltonian dynamics provides a Metropolis proposal for {p, q} which is accepted with the usual Metropolis acceptance procedure for the extended distribution pi(p, q).
>
> You then get a sample from pi(q) by simply ignoring the variables p since the marginal of the extended distribution is the target distribution, \int dp pi(p, q) = pi(q) \int dp pi(p | q) = pi(q).
>
> I haven't looked at your model in any depth, but if there is finite posterior density at rho = 1 then there will be problems sampling with HMC.  The problem is that when we transform rho to an unconstrained space the boundaries go to infinity, [0, 1] -> [-inf, inf].  If the posterior density is finite at rho = 1 then it will also be finite at rho_unconstrained = inf, and Hamiltonian dynamics falls apart when the Hamiltonian is non-zero at infinity.  Computationally it's easy to see why -- if the density is non-zero out there, then the chain needs to travel all the way out to infinity which would take an infinite amount of time, not to mention wreaking havoc on any numerical implementation.  This is case where using bouncing to constrain variables can help, but we haven't implemented that in Stan.
>
> -Mike

Hi Carlos: No, my simulation code doesn't have to do with adding a trend. That was just my silly deterministic way of generating random coefficients to test out how well the parameters are estimated.
It can be confusing because of the t-subscripting but the reduced form of the koyck model ( the one being coded in STAN )  is really just a  cross
 sectional regression. ( although there are issues with
correlation between regressor and noise term in estimating it as a regression but I shouldn't go into that here ). I write the model for each time t below:

y_1 = lambda* y_0 + lambda((1-p)* X_1 + epsilon_1
y_2 = lambda*y_1 + lambda(1-p)* X_2 + epsilon_2
y_3 = lambda * y_2 + lambda*(1-p)*X_3  + epsilon_3
.
.
.

the subscripts are t ( as in time ) but you can really just think of them as indices. So, I just incremented the X_t's by 1 each time in the code but that's not a trend model as you see from above. Just
different X coefficients in order to see how the parameters get estimated. If there was a second index in the y vector that was indexed by t, then that would be assuming some kind of trend.
If you want to think of above as a time series model,  you actually can think of it as an AR(1) with
an exogenous coefficient but that's not really a useful way to think of
it atleast in my opinion.
You can shuffle around the (X,y ) pairs in the code using "sample" in R and re-run the model and
you'll see that you'll get the same estimates. I'm not sure if that
explains your trend question. Let me know.

But, the true model ( what I refer to as the long form that is really the true model. short form is just a reparameterization in order to make estimation easier  ) underlying the short form above is actually a
lagged time series model but still with no time trend. Specifically:

y_t = beta*(sum from i = zero to infinity of (lambda^i *X_t-i) + epsilon_t  for every t

This is the really interesting formulation of the model and the way I like to think of it. ( I also sometimes think of it in the short form way but this one makes it more clear to me what's really happening ).

Note that It's the same model as the short form but re-written. This model captures ( or is supposed to capture anyway ) the lagged effects of X_t  on y_t over time. So, for example, say you had a shock X_t at time t where X_t was an abundance of dollars spent on advertising at time t. ( company is doing a special advertising push say at time t ). Also, suppose you let y_t denotes sales at time t. Then what this model tries to do is capture the lagged effect of this $ investment as time goes forward from time t. Since the weights are decaying as you go firhter back in time, it's assumes that as you go back further in time,
the effect on y_t decreases. So, it's kind of like a decreasing momentum model. But it's neat because most econometric/time series models don't handle effects that occur over time. They assume the effect is all at once.

If  you don't know which one to read, let me know and I can dig up something that's good and send you the title. I haven't looked at koyck papers about it in a good while but I've read many. The Koyck model is an econometric model that is I think top 5 or top 10 all time in econometric citations.  I hope this helped clear up what's going on in the code and the model.

The true use of the reduced form of the koyck model is to construct an estimable model with 3 parameters because, in its long form ( the one of the form beta * sum of infinite lags with each lag multiplied by weight lambda^i ), is extremely difficult to estimate. So, koyck figured the transformation out which leads to the reduced version which is what we're trying to estimate because it's also 3 parameters
but much easier to estimate.

Modeling Language

Command-Line

   estimation with Newton's method

RStan
* added method as.mcmc.list()

C++/Internal
* refactored math/agrad libs in C++ to separate files/includes,
   remove redundant code, more unit tests for existing code

Hi Michael : Below was a beautiful explanation. I think I'm getting closer and you're also correct that I was over thinking it or atleast wrongly thinking it !!!!. If you can bear with me and
just explain this last piece at your convenience, I'd appreciate it. ( this is not the trajectory stuff but that's a future battle ).  So, here goes. I will state what I think I understand first and then where my confusion
is. But, if I'm incorrect in where I think I'm correct, then please let me know that also of course.

In regular metropolis hastings, ( local, global, whatever ),  the proposal for the new state is generated using some proposal distribution. ( I'm aware of the difficulties of which one to choose and the variance issue etc ). Then, one  uses the acceptance step as a way to insure detailed balance. Finally, detailed balance implies convergence of the constructed markov chain.to <http://chain.to> the stationary distribution. Because of the way the acceptance prob is constructed, min(1, prob(new state)prob(old state|new state) divided by prob(old state)prob(new state|old state) ), this stationary distribution fortunately corresponds to the one we are trying to generate from in the first  place !!!! Good,  got that.

Now, in HMC, ( the last time I studied phyiscs was 1984 and there were no differential equations so there's going to be hand waving going on here ) we are trying to draw from the distribution of q which I denote
as p(q) but we actually have to two sets of variables, q and p, where the p are the artificial ones just introduced to make HMC work. We can stick to 1 dimensional p and q for what I'm asking here.

Now,  in HMC, the new proposal ( the next p and q)  is generated using the leapfrog steps which are a discretization of the dynamics implied by hamilton's equations. ( except the momentum is actually
generated randomly afterwards to get out of the contour of constant probability but I'll talk about probabilities later ) .  Okay, fine. Then, aside from the way the proposal is done, the acceptance step is exactly the same way it is in metropolis hastings : prob(acceptance of new state) = min(1, prob(new state)prob(old state|new state) divided by [ prob(old state)prob(new state|old state) ].

Then, using the same detailed balance balance argument, the acceptance step implies convergence of the constructed markov chain to the stationary distribution prob(p,q) = prob(p)prob(q|p). But independence
of p and q implies that you can just generate the joint sample of (p, q) and use the generated sample from q because that will converge to the marginal of q. Good. Got that.

But here's where I get lost. According to what I've read,  Prob(p,q) = e to the -[U(q) +K(p)]. ( picture lots of waving of hands here !!!! ).  Now, in the actual statistical problem, we are ultimately trying to sample from some (posterior) density p(q). Like in  the koyck model, we are trying to sample from p(rho, beta, sigma| data) so q = (rho,beta, sigma ).

 So in the actual HMC implementation,  one sets U(q) = - log(prob(rho, beta, sigma).  In this way since prob(p,q) = e to the -(U(q) +K(p)),  this reduces to prob(p,q) = p(q) * [e to the -K(p).]. So ( because of the independence of p and q,  as stated earlier),  the procedure ends up generating samples from the marginal,  prob(q) = prob(rho, beta, sigma) which is exactly what we wanted !!!! Good. Sort of got that,

But, when I read Radford Neal's material, I must be missing some kind of key relationship between the hamilton equations/leapfrog steps and the probabilities. How can one just out
of the seemingly  blue say that Prob(p,q) = e to the -[U(q) +K(p)]. Is that some kind of physical relationship implied by the hamiltonian equations themselves ? In other words, my question is,
do the hamiltonian equations somehow make that relation be true ? that prob(p,q) = e to the -[U(q) + K(p)]. If so, then I'll just accept it ( no pun intended ). I ask this because I don't see it all.
In statistics, one will just out of the blue say that such and such variable X is exponentially distributed or gamma distributed so that one can say that prob(X = x) = some density function. But then this has
to be tested for it's correctness. In HMC, one is stating a probability relationship of variables p and q that are being generated by a set of differential equations. So, I don't think it's an assumption
but rather some kind of by product of the equations ? Is that correct that it's just a fact ? This is my main confusion. if I can understand this, then I think I get it.

Then, to close the story, if it is factual, then is it the discretization of the hamiltonian equations that makes one need the acceptance step. I read somewhere that, if you didn't have to discretize, then you
wouldn't even need the acceptance step because detailed balance would hold exactly without the acceptance step. Again that has to do with the probabilities so it's probably related to the question above.

I guess to summarize I can say that I don't see how one can discretize a differential equation and then have that probability relation be true ? In fact, forget about discretizing. I don't see it even without discretization. But that's where my NULL physics background may be coming into play. Lastly, it's really nice of you to go out of your way to help me. Hopefully you'll be helping some others also ? Thank
you very much.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Mark

On Thursday, April 11, 2013 3:53:24 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> > D) I don't claim to be an HMC expert but I'm trying to think about something that my understanding is not 100 percent clear on so hear me out if you don't mind. Lennart says that the log posterior goes to
> > infinity as rho goes to 1. I'm not clear on how he knows that but, assuming it's true: could the problem then correspond to the example on pages 30-31 of "Probabilistic Inference Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo
> > Methods" by Radford Neal. If someone could take a look at that discussion and the picture in c). The density is spiking up in one place and the values of A in that place are all very low so MCMC sampling will
> > be problematic. I don''t know enough about HMC ( atleast yet. as time permits, I'm going back over then DUANE paper for the 38th time ) yet to say anything with confidence but maybe the problem has something to do with that which I think is what Lennart was saying ?
>
> It sounds like you're dramatically over-thinking HMC, so let me try to explain.
>
> In HMC you're not sampling from your target distribution pi(q), but rather an extended distribution pi(p, q) = pi(p | q) p (q).  Hamiltonian dynamics provides a Metropolis proposal for {p, q} which is accepted with the usual Metropolis acceptance procedure for the extended distribution pi(p, q).
>
> You then get a sample from pi(q) by simply ignoring the variables p since the marginal of the extended distribution is the target distribution, \int dp pi(p, q) = pi(q) \int dp pi(p | q) = pi(q).
>
> I haven't looked at your model in any depth, but if there is finite posterior density at rho = 1 then there will be problems sampling with HMC.  The problem is that when we transform rho to an unconstrained space the boundaries go to infinity, [0, 1] -> [-inf, inf].  If the posterior density is finite at rho = 1 then it will also be finite at rho_unconstrained = inf, and Hamiltonian dynamics falls apart when the Hamiltonian is non-zero at infinity.  Computationally it's easy to see why -- if the density is non-zero out there, then the chain needs to travel all the way out to infinity which would take an infinite amount of time, not to mention wreaking havoc on any numerical implementation.  This is case where using bouncing to constrain variables can help, but we haven't implemented that in Stan.
>
> -Mike

p(p,q) is a density that was defined (nor derived) by
the inventors of HMC.  Among other properties, the
definition has these pleasing features:

   1.  The marginal density p(q) of the position q is the
       distribution  we want to sample from (by construction).
       So if we can sample (p,q) from p(p,q), we can sample q
       from p(q).

   2.  The joint density p(p,q) decomposes into a separable
       Hamiltonian form.

In other words, my question is,
> do the hamiltonian equations somehow make that relation be true ? that prob(p,q) = e to the -[U(q) + K(p)]. If so, then
> I'll just accept it ( no pun intended ). I ask this because I don't see it all.

> In statistics, one will just out of the blue say that such and such variable X is exponentially distributed or gamma
> distributed

These are almost always modeling assumptions, which need
to be checked.

> ... is it the discretization of the hamiltonian equations that makes one
> need the acceptance step.

Yes.  If we could do the integral corresponding to the Hamiltonian
dynamics perfectly, the acceptance rate would be 100%.

The key to understanding why it maintains detailed balance is due
to volume preservation (this is the part that was tricky for me
to understand).

- Bob

It's very helpful to have the examples in .stan and .R files. Thanks!

I found them on github:

In this location, the "normal-mixture_k-sim.R" file has a typo in the last line:

           fit <- stan(file="normal_mixture_k.stan", data=("K","N","y"), iter=500, chains=1, init=0);

It should be:

           fit <- stan(file="normal_mixture_k.stan", data=c("K","N","y"), iter=500, chains=1, init=0);

I also tried chains=4, with interesting non-identifiability results - or, if the term "non-identifiable" is not accurate, at least the three components across chains are inter-changed, so while print(fit) with chains=1 gives accurate results, print(fit) with chains = 4 does not, although I imagine each chain gives sensible results (not checked yet).

messages.body_plain:
thanks bob. I'll print out below and read carefully. it's much appreciated. eventually I'll get back to playing with stan/koyck and report back ( will try Ben's idea also ) but I want to understand HMC
better first. have a good day.

On Saturday, April 13, 2013 2:11:16 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 4/13/13 8:18 AM, Mark Leeds wrote:
> ...
> > But, when I read Radford Neal's material, I must be missing some kind of key relationship between the hamilton
> > equations/leapfrog steps and the probabilities. How can one just out
> > of the seemingly  blue say that Prob(p,q) = e to the -[U(q) +K(p)]. Is that some kind of physical relationship implied
> > by the hamiltonian equations themselves ?
>
> p(p,q) is a density that was defined (nor derived) by
> the inventors of HMC.  Among other properties, the
> definition has these pleasing features:
>
>    1.  The marginal density p(q) of the position q is the
>        distribution  we want to sample from (by construction).
>        So if we can sample (p,q) from p(p,q), we can sample q
>        from p(q).
>
>    2.  The joint density p(p,q) decomposes into a separable
>        Hamiltonian form.
>
> In other words, my question is,
> > do the hamiltonian equations somehow make that relation be true ? that prob(p,q) = e to the -[U(q) + K(p)]. If so, then
> > I'll just accept it ( no pun intended ). I ask this because I don't see it all.
>
> > In statistics, one will just out of the blue say that such and such variable X is exponentially distributed or gamma
> > distributed
>
> These are almost always modeling assumptions, which need
> to be checked.
>
> > ... is it the discretization of the hamiltonian equations that makes one
> > need the acceptance step.
>
> Yes.  If we could do the integral corresponding to the Hamiltonian
> dynamics perfectly, the acceptance rate would be 100%.
>
> The key to understanding why it maintains detailed balance is due
> to volume preservation (this is the part that was tricky for me
> to understand).
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
bob: below was extremely helpful particularly when you said "DEFINED" by the inventors of HMC. I get it now I think: The construction of the hamiltionian form for the probabilities is really just a useful way to
say that the probabilities of the two variables ( p and q ) are independent. And, since the hamiltonian form ends up reducing to the density of the one we're interested in TIMES the density of the one we're
not interested in , it's irrelevant if the density of the second one is not true because we don't care about it anyway  !!!!!!!! really neat stuff. The leapfrog steps  are a construction for proposing from the joint of p and q but are connected to the hamiltonian construction through the gradients of the respective densities and therefore "consistent" with the hamiltonian.  WOW.   It feels good when the light goes on !!!!!

Thanks so much to everyone on this list for their patience and help, particularly , Michael, Bob and Ben. I will get back with STAN results but it may be a while because I have some other things currently going on.

messages.subject: nice discussion of priors in box and tiao
messages.subject_clean: nice discussion of priors in box and tiao
messages.body_plain:
I just figured I'd make a new post to let people know ( who don't already know ) that there's a very nice discussion of non-informative /locally uniform priors on page 21 and 25-31 of Box and Tiao. Ben, if you read that, it explains how the  joint prior in adl_gibbs.pdf  becomes 1/sigma. It turns out that the marginal priors for beta and lambda that result in that joint prior are called locally uniform priors.  ( but better to read that than to listen to my babblings ).  Not that the joint prior is adl_gibbs.pdf is necessarily a good joint prior but it does hold to the idea that the priors for all three parameters ( sigma, beta, and lambda ) be locally uniform.

I think the discussion in Box and Tiao may also be related to what Michael said about Hamiltonian dynamics having problems when a parameter in the model has mass near infinity. But I need to read adl_gibbs.pdf in detail
before I say or think any more on that. I'll be in touch and thanks to everyone for their great help.

messages.subject: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.subject_clean: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I would be curious to hear from you what are the strongest arguments to switch from using BUGS to Stan. For me its like comparing Windows to Linux and i do not argue about what to use, but seriously:

- Which type of problems are better solved in Stan?
- For which problems do we really need a HMC sampler, i.e. a sampler which avoids random walk? Or when are autocorrelations a problem in Gibbs, but not in HMC?
- Why should I use Stan if I only do a meta analysis with few data?

I am trying to compile some arguments to convince people to use Stan, but I was surprised to see how bad Stan performs for a mixture model (the eyes bugs example) - just as JAGS. So I am starting to think that JAGS altogether does a pretty good job at many problems.

Does it come down to raw speed for large data sets?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.subject_clean: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.body_plain:
I can't give the "best" arguments, but here are some reasons that I like Stan (and its community):

* C-like programming for flow control, data manipulation, and variable scoping
* It always converges for my models (when specified correctly).  No little knobs to turn to get good performance.
* Vectorized functions are very fast. I usually have too-much-data and relatively simple models.
* Distributions have sane parameterization (e.g. Normal distribution: precision vs. stddev)
* Very convenient to install and use with R
* Helpful ecosystem (ask a reasonable question, get a great answer)
* Open Development process (get patches as soon as posted to github)

There are some things that I wish Stan could do, and the Stan group is acutely aware of them (see their TO-DO list)

messages.subject_clean: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, April 16, 2013 4:21:18 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Dear list,
>
> I would be curious to hear from you what are the strongest arguments to switch from using BUGS to Stan. For me its like comparing Windows to Linux and i do not argue about what to use, but seriously:
>
> - Which type of problems are better solved in Stan?
> - For which problems do we really need a HMC sampler, i.e. a sampler which avoids random walk? Or when are autocorrelations a problem in Gibbs, but not in HMC?
> - Why should I use Stan if I only do a meta analysis with few data?
>
> I am trying to compile some arguments to convince people to use Stan, but I was surprised to see how bad Stan performs for a mixture model (the eyes bugs example) - just as JAGS. So I am starting to think that JAGS altogether does a pretty good job at many problems.
>
> Does it come down to raw speed for large data sets?

I would say it never comes down to raw speed. If you want to focus on performance, it should be effective sample size or effective sample size over wall time. Even then, I think Stan and BUGS calculate effective sample size differently, so doing an apples-to-apples comparison takes some work.

I think our goal is to make Stan the best general-purpose MCMC software, but we aren't there yet, and even if we were it would always be the case that other software would be best for a particular purpose. That said, I think a full comparison is a bit premature because Stan has only been in development for a couple of years and BUGS has been around for a couple of decades I think. So, Stan has a lot of room to grow, particularly in the near future when Mike's RMHMC stuff gets merged in and we can attack harder problems. I don't know if there is much left to do on the Gibbs sampling front, except to derive more full-conditional distributions.

Objectively, Stan (at the moment) can't do models with discrete unknowns (unless you can integrate them out) and BUGS can't do models that cannot be expressed as DAGs. Also, a Gibbs sampler can have a low effective sample size when the parameters are highly correlated. Stan currently has difficulty with parameters with very different scales, perhaps exacerbated when the parameters are highly correlated, but these can often be worked around with model reparameterizations. Also, RMHMC is supposed to overcome these problems.

Subjectively, I feel that Gibbs samplers encourage people to formulate their priors in ways that facilitate Gibbs sampling (e.g. normals, Wisharts, etc.) whereas with other MCMC methods, users are free to choose whatever prior reflects their beliefs. Also, I have long been frustrated by BUGS's mostly scalar algebra approach to specifying models, whereas Stan builds on Eigen's matrix library and the STL. It's not just a matter of wall time, but also a matter of convenience and clarity of specifying models, particularly models with many parameters (e.g. X * beta versus x1[i] * beta1 + x2[i] * beta2 ...)

Those seem like the most major points to me.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.body_plain:
> On Tuesday, April 16, 2013 4:21:18 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
 >
 >     Dear list,
 >
 >     I would be curious to hear from you what are the strongest arguments to switch from using BUGS to Stan.

Could you let us know what you're looking for in
a sampling package?  We're always open to suggestions
on how to make Stan better.

We like BUGS and JAGS and have used them for years
ourselves!

I'd be very curious to hear about this issue from a user
perspective (and thanks to Eric Brown for already
responding [by the way, Martyn Plummer provides good
advice on the JAGS mailing list, too;  I haven't looked
at OpenBUGS or WinBUGS mailing lists]).

There's an appendix in the manual that goes over some
comparisons with BUGS/JAGS on a more technical level.

We've been meaning to run some large scale comparisons
for ages, but we keep spending our time working on Stan
instead.  We just recruited a student today that's going
to work on comparisons over the summer (it's a bigger project than it
sounds to do this sensibly, with varying scale of data,
of parameters, of data complexity, of model complexity, the
need to deal for initializations and variance of run
times and effective sample sizes with different starting points,
the decision of whether to use the minimum n_eff as the measure
and whether to measure second (centered) moments for convergence
as well as the first moments, etc.).

For some conjugate models like the Rats example from BUGS
volume 1, we're still finding JAGS a bit faster than Stan (I'm guessing
a factor of 2 or 3 at this point).  For some models we're seeing
big advantages for Stan.   But until we have more information (see
last paragraph), we haven't been shouting this from the rooftops.

Ben's point about measuring effective sample size is very
important and will be more important with RM-HMC and Geometric
NUTS, which are slower per iteration but much better at mixing
and converging.  (And for effective sample size, you have to be careful
with mixture models, because R-hat no longer makes sense on
the non-identifiable components;  in general, highly multimodal
posteriors are problematic for most samplers and optimizers,
with more problems the more multimodal they are).

The R-hat built into RStan is more conservative (due to
splitting the chains in half) than in R2WinBUGS or R2jags.
RStan also draws prettier pictures.  But that's not a feature of
BUGS or JAGS.  You can use our posterior analysis with BUGS/JAGS
output or vice-versa.

Here's a list of some issues off the top of my head:

One, Stan declares and types its variables and provides more
extensive warning messages for errors.  This is not a small
consideration when developing complex models.  I find the types
and declarations make the models (and error messages) more
understandable.  BUGS models can be used with any of the nodes
as parameters with the decision made at runtime; this makes a
single BUGS model more flexible.

As to syntax/operations, I also like our MATLAB-like
matrix operations.  We'll be vectorizing almost all of the
operations in the language in the coming months.

Two, Stan is more imperative.  Local variables can be reused
and sums can be accumulated in loops.  You can directly code
your (perhaps not built into Stan) log probability function
with mathematical functions and the lp__ variable.  This lets
you encode the functionality in JAGS's GLM module directly
in a Stan model.

Two point Five, Stan lets you specify the joint probability
or the posterior or anything in between -- as long as the
log probability function is proportional to the posterior, you're
OK.

Three, Stan is currently providing optimizers for the same
modeling language and these will get better.  (Warning:  Andrew's not
a fan of MAP or MLE estimates.)  Stan's flexible modeling language
lets you code maximal marginal posteriors with a little work.

Four, Stan should be much less sensitive to initial values
than BUGS/JAGS.  This is, of course, problem dependent.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I've found that my models which used vectors for data in count models break when upgrading from 1.2.0 to 1.3.0.

So I've had to change
data {
   int N;
   vector[N] y;
}
...
model {
   y ~ poisson_log(log_mu);
}

to
data {
   int N;
   int y[N];
}
...
model {
   y ~ poisson_log(log_mu);
}

Seems like a logical change since vectors are real-valued instead of integers, just thought I'd point it out in case others run into similar backwards compatibility issues.

messages.subject: bug in inv_cloglog formula
messages.body_plain:
The formula for inv_cloglog is wrong.  It should be:

   inv_cloglog(y) =  1 - exp(-exp(y))

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.body_plain:
If Bugs is solving your problems, no reason to switch away from it.  We wrote Stan in part becuase Bugs was choking on certain problems with complex structure (such as multilevel models with unknown covariance matrices) and other problems that were too big for Bugs (such as our tree-ring model).  And when Bugs doesn't work it's hard to do much with it.
A

>

>

messages.subject: Re: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.subject_clean: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.body_plain:
I've converted most of my MCMC work to Stan, and I've started evangelizing it on my campus. The reasons I prefer it are mainly:

(1) Easier to debug than JAGS. Partly this is because of the error messages and partly because the explicit typing forces me to think more.

(2) I work with some non-standard models that require some fiddling to build the likelihoods. For example, experience weighted attraction models of learning need some looping to compute memory effects, and those are rather slow in JAGS, but lightning fast in Stan. Ordered logistic models also are much faster in Stan, but rather a pain in JAGS.

(3) I don't like conjugate priors! Stan frees me to use the priors I want for inference, not the priors I need for estimation.

All that said, missing data imputation is quite a chore in Stan. I expect as array slicing gets added, it'll be easier.

Hey everyone, I'm back with a new version of this model!  The good news is that all of your suggestions really sped things up, it took ~2 days to finish, down from ~4 days from the original.  I probably don't need as many iterations, so it can go down even more in the future.

The current model is attached.  One improvement I'm trying to make (as suggested by Bob and others earlier today) is to pass all of the group variables in as a single matrix instead of the separate vectors, in order to improve readability of the model.  I started doing this but realized a problem: all of the alpha_* parameters are of variable length, due to the different number of levels in each of these groups.  Because of this, there can be no single matrix that can hold all the alphas.  Is that correct?

If so, I wonder if it would be worth implementing a new data structure in future versions of Stan that would allow this functionality -- something like lists in R.  My C++ days are long behind me, but I remember linked lists and the like, maybe that could be done here ... spoken as someone who admittedly has no idea how complicated it would be.

Thanks,

-Yair

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Reasons to switch from any BUGS to Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am interested in the user perspective as I want to convince other people to switch to Stan. The bigger the community the better. A comparison between the samplers is indeed a bigger project, I am looking forward to the results of your student.

I agree with the points raised so far, i.e. not being forced to think in terms of a DAG makes life a lot easier.

If I understood you guys correctly, then in Stan there is no advantage of using a conjugate prior, correct? So I am free to use anything I think makes sense? That's a good point for using Stan as I never like restrictions due to the sampler.

The only thing I really miss in Stan is ode support, but as I heard this is on the wishlist already. Furthermore, I am mostly interested in solving PKPD models which means effectivley to estimate growth rates of exponentials which are summed together. I already coded such a model and it works, but Stan is not awfully efficient here - the ESS is about 1/10 of the total sample size. I was playing with the thought to code some of the analytical solutions as functions in the Stan library. Is there an obvious place to do these extension and what is the best way to use such functions in Stan? I.e. is Stan extensible in some sense such that one can think of writing a PKPD Stan library?

Another feature which would be very handy is to have views into vectors. I.e. in my problems I have to loop over my data because I only need a certain subset of the underlying vector, but as I know the indices I need each time in advance, a view should make it more expressive and possibly faster. For example let v be a vector of length 10, a statement v[i:i+5] with i=2 would be nice to have.

This is (besides ode) only minor stuff and Stan is a great piece of software! I am really looking forward to where Stan is going, especially with this RMHMC...

Best,

Sebastian

On Tue, Apr 16, 2013 at 10:12 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> > On Tuesday, April 16, 2013 4:21:18 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> >
> >     Dear list,
> >
> >     I would be curious to hear from you what are the strongest arguments to switch from using BUGS to Stan.
>
> Could you let us know what you're looking for in
> a sampling package?  We're always open to suggestions
> on how to make Stan better.
>
> We like BUGS and JAGS and have used them for years
> ourselves!
>
> I'd be very curious to hear about this issue from a user
> perspective (and thanks to Eric Brown for already
> responding [by the way, Martyn Plummer provides good
> advice on the JAGS mailing list, too;  I haven't looked
> at OpenBUGS or WinBUGS mailing lists]).
>
> There's an appendix in the manual that goes over some
> comparisons with BUGS/JAGS on a more technical level.
>
> We've been meaning to run some large scale comparisons
> for ages, but we keep spending our time working on Stan
> instead.  We just recruited a student today that's going
> to work on comparisons over the summer (it's a bigger project than it
> sounds to do this sensibly, with varying scale of data,
> of parameters, of data complexity, of model complexity, the
> need to deal for initializations and variance of run
> times and effective sample sizes with different starting points,
> the decision of whether to use the minimum n_eff as the measure
> and whether to measure second (centered) moments for convergence
> as well as the first moments, etc.).
>
> For some conjugate models like the Rats example from BUGS
> volume 1, we're still finding JAGS a bit faster than Stan (I'm guessing
> a factor of 2 or 3 at this point).  For some models we're seeing
> big advantages for Stan.   But until we have more information (see
> last paragraph), we haven't been shouting this from the rooftops.
>
> Ben's point about measuring effective sample size is very
> important and will be more important with RM-HMC and Geometric
> NUTS, which are slower per iteration but much better at mixing
> and converging.  (And for effective sample size, you have to be careful
> with mixture models, because R-hat no longer makes sense on
> the non-identifiable components;  in general, highly multimodal
> posteriors are problematic for most samplers and optimizers,
> with more problems the more multimodal they are).
>
> The R-hat built into RStan is more conservative (due to
> splitting the chains in half) than in R2WinBUGS or R2jags.
> RStan also draws prettier pictures.  But that's not a feature of
> BUGS or JAGS.  You can use our posterior analysis with BUGS/JAGS
> output or vice-versa.
>
> Here's a list of some issues off the top of my head:
>
> One, Stan declares and types its variables and provides more
> extensive warning messages for errors.  This is not a small
> consideration when developing complex models.  I find the types
> and declarations make the models (and error messages) more
> understandable.  BUGS models can be used with any of the nodes
> as parameters with the decision made at runtime; this makes a
> single BUGS model more flexible.
>
> As to syntax/operations, I also like our MATLAB-like
> matrix operations.  We'll be vectorizing almost all of the
> operations in the language in the coming months.
>
> Two, Stan is more imperative.  Local variables can be reused
> and sums can be accumulated in loops.  You can directly code
> your (perhaps not built into Stan) log probability function
> with mathematical functions and the lp__ variable.  This lets
> you encode the functionality in JAGS's GLM module directly
> in a Stan model.
>
> Two point Five, Stan lets you specify the joint probability
> or the posterior or anything in between -- as long as the
> log probability function is proportional to the posterior, you're
> OK.
>
> Three, Stan is currently providing optimizers for the same
> modeling language and these will get better.  (Warning:  Andrew's not
> a fan of MAP or MLE estimates.)  Stan's flexible modeling language
> lets you code maximal marginal posteriors with a little work.
>
> Four, Stan should be much less sensitive to initial values
> than BUGS/JAGS.  This is, of course, problem dependent.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Speeding Up Multinomial Logistic Regressions in Stan
messages.subject_clean: Speeding Up Multinomial Logistic Regressions in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm working on a problem that will eventually require a slightly complicated multilevel multinomial logistic regression model; so I'm naturally hoping to fit this model in Stan. Unfortunately, even for very straightforward multinomial logistic regression models, Stan seems to be dramatically slower than some of the alternatives, especially the MCMCmnl function in MCMCpack.

For example, I've fit a simple multinomial logit regression using an example data set from the MCMCpack package (the "Nethvote" dataset). Running the code from the manual (literally copy-and-paste), the Stan model takes about 20 minutes for a single chain of 1,000 iterations on my laptop (a fairly new MacBook Pro). By contrast, corresponding MCMCpack function takes about 3 seconds for 1,000 iterations, and about 45 seconds for the recommended 100,000 iterations. Of course, I realize that the Stan sampler can be slow in certain situations---especially relative to the M-H draws that MCMCpack uses---but I didn't expect a several order-of-magnitude difference between the run times. (Note that I've heard reports from several others about how slow multinomial logit regression in Stan can be.) Finally, I've also tried inputing the covariates as vectors rather than matrices, but didn't find a marked increase in speed.

I've attached the example code, which includes the "sessionInfo()" output. Hopefully there is an obvious fix to this problem, as it'd be great to use Stan for the more complex multinomial model that I'd like to fit!

Thanks in advance for the help.

Best,
Avi Feller

messages.body_plain:
There are a couple things to keep in mind.

1) The example models in the manual are often written with
expositional clarity in mind, not speed.  There is a section on
improving performance through vectorization which you should check
out.  That model can be made to run a fair bit faster, particularly
for large amounts of data/variables.  (We should probably provide a
library of "clear" and "optimized" examples for cases like this...)
If you need help vectorizing things, let us know.

2) MCMCmnl uses RW Metropolis and/or slice sampling.  As a rule, Stan
will require far fewer samples than MCMCmnl to achieve a certain level
of accuracy.  Or, to put it another way, 1 iteration of Stan is worth
a lot more than one iteration of MCMCmnl.

3) Stan may be be beaten by specially designed packages which target
very specific forms of models.  This is the nature of the tradeoff
between generality and speed.  That said, if you take 2) into account
when comparing results, Stan can still sometimes beat out specialized
packages.

Cheers,
Marcus

Marcus and Michael (et al.),

First, thank you both for the prompt and thoughtful responses. I had already been thinking about Marcus's second and third points, but I definitely appreciate the need to reiterate them---they're important to keep in mind!

Michael's suggestion to check ESS is a good one. However, it only confirms my previous suspicions: the ESS for the MCMCpack estimates are generally between 11,000-12,000 (based on 100,000 iterations) and took about 50 seconds to estimate; the corresponding ESS for estimates from a single 1,000 iteration chain from Stan are between 250 and 300, but took about 22 minutes (~1350 seconds). So ESS/time is extremely unfavorable to Stan using the code from the manual.

Of course, I do understand that the MCMCmnl function was specifically tailored to this problem, but this still seems like a fairly dramatic asymmetry.

As for point #1, I had previously tried vectorizing/optimizing the Stan code but kept hitting roadblocks (to be fair, I'm fairly new to Stan so maybe I'm just doing a poor job!). Specifically, it appears as if the "softmax" can only take vectors, rather than matrices---in other words, Stan can only pass vectors of linear predictors to the softmax function one observation at a time. I had considered implementing something more complicated to work around this issue, but decided it made more sense to just email the Stan list directly.

In short, I'd very much welcome your suggestions for speeding up the example multinomial logit code. And again, I hope I'm just missing something else obvious (it certainly wouldn't be the first time).

Avi

messages.body_plain:
Today, we've got bupkis (i.e., nothing).

The new edition of "Bayesian Data Analysis" (which is
now complete and going through a final revision) contains
a chapter on the alternatives, including DIC, WAIC
and leave-one-out cross-validation.

There are two coding challenges for Stan.

First, we need to be able to isolate likelihoods (either
for all the data for DIC or item-by-item for WAIC).  The
likelihood is not even necessarily specified directly in
a Stan model, much less possible to infer automatically.
For instance, you can write a Stan model using an
analytic posterior without using an expression for the
data likelihood.

Second, we need cross-chain, cross-sample statistics like
sample means to be fed back into the model's likelihood
function.

Cross-validation you can set up on your own from the
outside, but again, if you care about likelihood, you'll
have to write out the likelihood explicitly and save
it as a generated quantity.  You can isolate ("cut" in
BUGS terms) the new-data predictions, too, by also putting those
in the generated quantities block.  But then you'd have
to run something like RStan, pull out the means, then feed
them back into the model.

We should at least set up an example of how to do this, but
it's never going to be automatic in the same way as BUGS
computes DIC.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the report.

Have you checked the two models produce the same answers
(within MCMC error)?   If MCMCmnl is working for you,
there's really no reason to switch to Stan if you don't
need Stan's modeling flexibility.

We would, of course, like to make Stan faster.

Would you mind sharing your data?   We're collecting
benchmark problems.  Or at least telling
us the sizes and if the predictors were standardized and
how much correlation there was among the predictors?

You're right that there's no vectorization of categorical
or of sofmax yet.  But that's not the key to speeding this
model up.

As to the specialization of the code, what we really need
to do is write a multi_logit distribution so that your model likelihood:

    for (n in 1:N)
       y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta * x[n]));

can be written as:

    y ~ multi_logit(beta, x);

For simple multinomial regression, all the derivatives take
very simple analytic forms for the likelihood and coding
this function this way would be as much as 20 times faster
than what's there now.  Which would leave us only a factor
of 20 or so slower :-)

I'll put it on the to-do list.  This is the kind of
thing we really want to make faster, so it's a fairly
high priority, and it's independent of all of our other
work, so we should be able to get to it right away.
(In fact, Marcus just put in a bunch of improvements like
this for Gaussian process models so as to compute their
covariance matrices faster and remove redundant solver
calls.)

Your model as is could be sped up by declaring x as a matrix:

and transforming what you have:

   for (k in 1:K)
     for (d in 1:D)
       beta[k,d] ~ normal(0,5);
   for (n in 1:N)
     y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta * x[n]));

to first declare x as a matrix:

   matrix[N,K] x;

and then redefining the model to:

   model {
     vector[N] beta_x;
     beta_x <- beta * (5 * x);
     for (k in 1:K)
       beta_raw[k] ~ normal(0,1);
     for (n in 1:N)
       y[n] ~ categorical(beta_x[n]);
   }

It'd be even faster if you scaled the data
instead of multiplying x by 5 each time in this
loop.  You could either do that with the inputs or
in a transformed data block.  But it should be pretty
fast because 5 and x do not involve parameters (why
I grouped the expression so oddly).

- Bob

On 4/19/13 2:24 PM, Jack Tanner wrote:
> Bob, I'm awfully confused by your model redefinition. Why the multiplication by 5? How is beta_raw related to anything?
> Could you walk through this redefinition? Thanks in advance.

There's a section in the manual on reparameterization that should help.

In short, if beta is a parameter, then the statement:

    beta ~ normal(0,5);

is equivalent to declaring beta_raw a parameter and
defining beta in terms of beta_raw by:

    beta_raw ~ normal(0,1);
    beta <- beta_raw * 5;

So you make beta_raw the parameter, then scale it by 5 when
using it.  You can define beta as above (you'll need to make it
a local variable, or you can make it a transformed parameter if
you want to print it).  Or you can just fold
it into the expression where it's used, which I did.  Note
that:

    beta * x[n]  == beta_raw * 5 * x[n]

Associating (5 * x[n]) is faster because there's no
parameter involved.

- Bob

Subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding Up Multinomial Logistic Regressions in Stan

Marcus and Michael (et al.),

First, thank you both for the prompt and thoughtful responses. I had already been thinking about Marcus's second and third points, but I definitely appreciate the need to reiterate them---they're important to keep in mind!

Michael's suggestion to check ESS is a good one. However, it only confirms my previous suspicions: the ESS for the MCMCpack estimates are generally between 11,000-12,000 (based on 100,000 iterations) and took about 50 seconds to estimate; the corresponding ESS for estimates from a single 1,000 iteration chain from Stan are between 250 and 300, but took about 22 minutes (~1350 seconds). So ESS/time is extremely unfavorable to Stan using the code from the manual.

Of course, I do understand that the MCMCmnl function was specifically tailored to this problem, but this still seems like a fairly dramatic asymmetry.

As for point #1, I had previously tried vectorizing/optimizing the Stan code but kept hitting roadblocks (to be fair, I'm fairly new to Stan so maybe I'm just doing a poor job!). Specifically, it appears as if the "softmax" can only take vectors, rather than matrices---in other words, Stan can only pass vectors of linear predictors to the softmax function one observation at a time. I had considered implementing something more complicated to work around this issue, but decided it made more sense to just email the Stan list directly.

In short, I'd very much welcome your suggestions for speeding up the example multinomial logit code. And again, I hope I'm just missing something else obvious (it certainly wouldn't be the first time).

Many thanks,

Avi

> a lot more than one iteration of MCMCmnl.

Exactly.  Can you calculate the ESS for each method, in particular ESS / time?

data {

The chapter on implementing your own distributions
covers how to do this.

On 4/21/13 10:51 PM, Mark Leeds wrote:
>
> Hi everyone: I looked in the STAN manual but I couldn't find an example of what I'm trying to do so that's why I'm
> asking here. Now that I understand the problem more clearly, ( adl_gibbs2.pdf was a real eye opener ), the fix they
> recommend for dealing with the ridge at lambda = 1 is to set the following priors for the parameters.
>
> lambda should be set to be proportional to (1-lambda)^2. ( originally, it's improper uniform but this results in the
> ridge at lambda = 1 ).

If this is what you want, you just add the log probability
up to a proportion that doesn't depend on params, so that's just:

    lp__ <- lp__ + 2 * log1m(lambda);

Note that log1m(x) = log(1 - x), but is more arithmetically stable.

> sigmasquared should be proportional to 1/sigmasquared  ( log of sigmasquared is improper uniform. same as always ).

If the parameter is sigmasquared, that's

   lp__ <- lp__ - log(sigmasiquared);

> beta should be ~ k ( some constant. i.e: improper uniform prior. same as always ).

You don't need to do anything for this one.

> The revised prior on lambda should  eliminate the ridge in the posterior density  for (beta,lambda). ( see
> adl_gibbs2.pdf for details ).
>
> But is there a way to implement the above in STAN. I remember reading somewhere in the manual or in Ben's posts that if
> you don't specify priors, then they will be improper and flat but

"Stan" isn't an acronym, so it's not capitalized.

> A) Will STAN automatically know to set the flat improper on log(sigmasquared) and not sigmasquared. ( box and tiao
> explains why it should be on log sigmasquared ).

No.  If you declare

parameters {
   real<lower=0> sigmasquared;
}

That implies an improper flat prior on sigmasquared,
not on log(sigmasquared).

You need to work out the change of variable to put a flat
proper on log(sigmasquared).  If it works out to
p(sigmasquared) propto 1/sigmasquared, then you need what
I wrote above.  (I'm not quite up to working out changes
of variables in my head.)

> B) is it possible to set the prior on lambda to be proportional to (1-lambda)^2.  I realize that I can set the prior to
> a density with a parameter (1-lambda^2) but then the mathematical description of the
> cancelling out of the ridge in adl_gibbs2.pdf will no longer necessarily hold. So, I'd prefer to just be proportional to
> (1-lambda)^2.

Yes, no problem.  See above.  But if you want to allow (1-lambda)
to be negative, you have to be careful not to do what I did
above because you'll try to take the log of a negative.
Instead, use:

    lp__ <- lp__ + 2 * log(abs(1 - lambda));

You can't take the log of a negative number, of course.

> I tried the code below but STAN was not happy about not seeing a density.  I get

In Stan's defense, it is a programming language so you have to
follow its syntax to make its happy.  This isn't legal:

 >    lambda ~ (1-lambda)^2;     // fix according to adl_gibbs.pdf

Only named distributions are allowed after the twiddle.

What you want is to increment lp__ as described in the
custom probability function chapter of the manual.

- Bob

take a look at it, it's appreciated. The intention of the Stan  code for the 3 parameters, sigmasquared, beta and lambda respectively was for

A) sigmasquared to be restricted between zero and infinity and have the prior for sigmasquared be 1/sigmasquared.

B) beta to be unrestricted  and have its prior be flat and improper.

C) lambda to be restricted between 0 and 1 and have its prior be (1-lambda)^2.

Based on your previous useful explanation, I think that's what the code  at the bottom of this posting does. It's essentially an attempt at implementing the fix to the ridge at lambda = 1 problem described in adl_gibbs2.pdf. ( I also tried the version where beta1mlambda is made into one variable and then divided by (1-lambda) in the generated quantities section but that didn't work either ).

I just have a couple of questions because I have not dared to try to open the hood of Stan.  I've written code in C and C++, more C than C++, but I would need infrastructure training/tutelage to get involved with going inside of STAN. My guess is that this would require more time than the Stan team has time for at the moment.

1) Does Stan construct the U(x) = -log(p(x) symbolically ? for example, similarly to how mathematica would construct an expression.  I ask because this "fix" described in adl_gibbs2.pdf might be specific to the gibbs sampling framework. I don't know enough about the details of Stan to know whether the fix should work in Stan also. Essentially, atleast in the gibba sampling framework,  by giving that prior above to lambda, the (1-lambda) in the denominator of posterior density of beta conditional on lambda gets zapped and one ends up with (1-lambda) in the numerator which is fine because the density of beta conditional on lambda = 1 becomes zero. But I'm not sure if, in Stan,  U(x) gets constructed symbolically using the prior for lambda. Michael mention earlier that the lambda parameter
gets unconstrained so that the unconstrained version is on the interval [-inf, +inf] but I don't see how that happens. If it does, then doesn't posterior density need to be modified ?

2) Does the Stan team ever offer tutoring/training sessions for Stan newbies who have a decent amount of experience programming but no experience dealing with something the size and nature of
Stan. I'd like to understand Stan in more depth and I think the only way to accomplish that would be to get inside it.

Thanks for your great help. If the code below seems fine to you, then I may have hit another brick wall with the koyck model. But I'm used to that happening with Mr. Koyck.

set.seed(123)

#sigmasquared <- 1.0

#====================================

#====================================
#beta <- 1.0;
#lambda <- 0.75

#sigmasquared <- 1.0

#====================================
# GOOD: 2.7
#====================================
#beta <- 2.6;
#lambda <- 0.75

#sigmasquared <- 1.

#====================================
# STILL SO SO : 0.3
#====================================
#beta <- 0.5;
#lambda <- 0.75

#sigmasquared <- 1.0

#====================================
# OKAY:  0.8
#====================================
#beta <- 1.0;
#lambda <- 0.70

#sigmasquared <- 1.0

#====================================
# GOOD: 2.4
#====================================
#beta <- 2.6;
#lambda <- 0.70

#sigmasquared <- 1.0

#====================================
# GOOD: 0.4
#====================================
#beta <- 0.5;
#lambda <- 0.70

#sigmasquared <- 1.0
#===========================================

y <- rep(NA,T);

y[1] <- rnorm(1,beta * (1 - lambda) * x[1], sqrt(sigmasquared));

for (t in 2:T)

  y[t] <- rnorm(1, beta * (1 - lambda) * x[t] + lambda * y[t-1], sqrt(sigmasquared));

fit <- stan(file="koyck_paperb.stan", data=c("T","y","x"), iter=1000, chains=4);
print(fit)

#=====================================================================================
# STAN CODE FOR IMPLEMENTING RIDGE FIX DESCRIBED IN ADL_GIBBS2.pdf. PRIOR ON LAMBDA
# IS (1-LAMBDA)^2, BETA IS IMPROPER AND FLAT, SIGMASQUARED IS ~ 1/SIGMASQUARED
#=====================================================================================

data {
  int<lower=0> T; // number of time points
  real y[T]; // output at time t
  real x[T]; // predictor for time t
}
parameters {

  real beta;  // part of x coeff
  real <lower=0, upper=1> lambda; // lagged coeff
  real <lower=0> sigmasquared; // noise scale
}

model {
  y[1] ~  normal(beta*(1-lambda) * x[1], sqrt(sigmasquared));

  for (t in 2:T)

    y[t] ~ normal( beta*(1-lambda) * x[t] + lambda * y[t-1],sqrt(sigmasquared));

  lp__<- lp__ + 2 * log1m(lambda);

  lp__<- lp__  - log(sigmasquared);

}
#============================================================================================================

How so?

> I just have a couple of questions because I have not dared to try to open the hood of Stan.  I've written code in C and C++, more C than C++, but I would need infrastructure training/tutelage to get involved with going inside of STAN. My guess is that this would require more time than the Stan team has time for at the moment.

The problems you are having are not really C++ problems.

> 1) Does Stan construct the U(x) = -log(p(x) symbolically ? for example, similarly to how mathematica would construct an expression.

No, it's all double precision numerics.

> I ask because this "fix" described in adl_gibbs2.pdf might be specific to the gibbs sampling framework. I don't know enough about the details of Stan to know whether the fix should work in Stan also. Essentially, atleast in the gibba sampling framework,  by giving that prior above to lambda, the (1-lambda) in the denominator of posterior density of beta conditional on lambda gets zapped and one ends up with (1-lambda) in the numerator which is fine because the density of beta conditional on lambda = 1 becomes zero.

It's the same information matrix regardless of whether you are doing Gibbs or HMC, so any numeric problems would be essentially the same in both cases.

> But I'm not sure if, in Stan,  U(x) gets constructed symbolically using the prior for lambda. Michael mention earlier that the lambda parameter
> gets unconstrained so that the unconstrained version is on the interval [-inf, +inf] but I don't see how that happens. If it does, then doesn't posterior density need to be modified ?

For every parameter in Stan with constrained support, there is an unconstrained primitive parameter that you don't see but which is actually the space that Stan is sampling from. In the case of a parameter constrained to be between 0 and 1 (such as lambda), the unconstrained parameter is the output of the standard inverse logistic CDF. Conversely, the standard logistic CDF transforms the unconstrained parameter to the (0,1) interval.

> 2) Does the Stan team ever offer tutoring/training sessions for Stan newbies who have a decent amount of experience programming but no experience dealing with something the size and nature of
> Stan. I'd like to understand Stan in more depth and I think the only way to accomplish that would be to get inside it.

So far, no, but probably some time in the future. Basically, the model that you posted yields a sampler that doesn't move, which can be verified by doing

apply(fit, "chains", FUN = function(x) length(unique(as.data.frame(x)))) / nrow(fit) # acceptance rates

which are all 0.008 when I do it, which ideally should be around 0.6. Another thing to do is

pairs(fit)

which shows that the two dimensional density plot of beta and lambda is sort of a triangle (not good). This suggests that we need to reparameterize to get better geometry, so I would be interested to see what combining beta and 1 - lambda into beta1mlambda would do.

Ben

And not even necessarily Stan problems.  It's about
the shape of your posterior and identifiability.  So it's really
a stats problem.

Are you sure Gibbs can fit your data?

Have you tried fitting simpler models?  Or using simulated

>     1) Does Stan construct the U(x) = -log(p(x) symbolically ? for example, similarly to how mathematica would construct

I'm not sure what you mean by construct U(x).  It's never constructed
per se --- it corresponds to a program.

So if I write

   U(theta) = -log bernoulli(y|theta)

then it gets translated into Stan roughly as:

   double log_prob(double theta, bool y) {
      return -log(y ? theta : 1-theta);
   }

Is that symbolic or numerical?  Of course evaluating the value
involves numerical processing.

The gradients are computed symbolically on a line-by-line
basis using algorithmic (aka automatic) differentiation.
This calculates up to machine precision unlike finite diffs.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Prior on transformed parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Stan lets you write whatever you want.  The statement

    a ~ normal(mu,sigma);

just translates to:

    lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log(a,mu,sigma);

If you use a sampling statement with ~ and the element
on the left is a transformed parameter, then you have
to add the (log) Jacobian adjustment to lp__.

I'm going to go in right now and add a warning to that
effect in the parser --- we've been meaning to do that
for ages.

There's an example in the manual chapter on defining
new distributions where we show how to do this with
lognormal.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, April 24, 2013 7:27:39 PM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:
> The distribution indeed requires the Kronecker product, so I've followed Ben's suggestion and programmed it element by element. It's not fast, but will have to do for the time being ;) Thank you for taking a look!

Glad it is somewhat functional. In a case like a multivariate normal, you might be able to speed it up a little bit by being clever with the products. So, if you need (in R notation)

t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y

you end up repeatedly post-multiplying Lambda by segments of y and scaling those by elements of D - a * W. Particularly if D - a * W is sparse, you could squeeze out some efficiency gains by using temporaries.

This is one reason why Stan would need a really good implementation of Kronecker products to realize performance improvements, as opposed to merely having a convenient syntax for using the Kronecker product in Eigen.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Prior on transformed parameters?
messages.body_plain:
On 4/26/13 2:56 AM, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Thanks Bob!
>
> A warning here is very helpful to catch unwanted mistakes.

Right -- we'd been meaning to include one for ages but
I only recently added the necessary information to the parser
to do the check.

> I understand that putting a prior on a parameter or
> transformed parameter makes conceptually no difference and both approaches can result in a properly setup model.
> However, to me it looks like the policy should be that priors are on parameters only. So many thanks for a warning here
> - it will keep at least me from making my own mistakes...

Under the hood, a Stan model defines an unnormalized
conditional probability of parameters given data.

Sometimes it's convenient to define a transformation
of a parameter and put the prior on that or vice-versa.

For example, suppose you have a Dirichlet variate
K-vector alpha, with alpha[k] > 0.  You can reparameterize
in terms of a K-simplex theta and a total count alpha_sum > 0.

   alpha = alpha_sum * theta

   alpha_sum = sum(alpha)

   theta = alpha / sum(alpha)

Now suppose we want to express the prior on the transformed
parameters:

   alpha_sum ~ exp(a)
   theta ~ dirichlet(beta);

We can do this in Stan with either (alpha) or (alpha_sum,theta)
as the declared parameters.  If we take alpha to be the declared
parameters, we need to apply a Jacobian adjustment.  If (alpha_sum,theta)
are the declared parameters, we define alpha in terms of them and don't
need an adjustment.

- Bob

Sooo, let me consider two examples. The first one would be an stochastic search, where you have a bunch of variables, and you do not know which variables should enter as a regressors in a model, for example. Imagine that we have some data, Y, and we consider 3 regressors, X1, X2, and X2, with associated coefficients b1,b2 and b3. Then, we would like to model,

Y ~ normal(d1*b1*X1 + d2*b2*X2 + d3*b3*X3, sigma)

d1,d2 and d3 are binary variables that turn on or off the contribution of the variables X1, X2 and X3, respectively. If we model them as Bernouilli distributions, then the posterior mean of the parameters gives us the probability that the variable Xi should be included in the model. This is a very very very simple model, and obviously, can be done using other methods. But if we have tons of variables/combinations of variables, I guess that this procedure might help...

The second example is a state-space model. We can consider for example, a stochastic volatility model, with
Y[n]~normal(mu,exp(h[n]/2))
h[n]~h[n-1]+J[n]*hnoise
hnoise~normal(0,sigmah)
In this case, J[n] is again a binary variable. If J[n]=0, then h remains the same as in the previous period, while if J[n]=1, then (log) volatility changes by the amount hnoise

Thanks!

> and you do not know which variables should enter as a regressors in a model, for example. Imagine that we have some

> model,

> Y ~ normal(d1*b1*X1 + d2*b2*X2 + d3*b3*X3, sigma)

This is the one we haven't figured out how to do.  It's
easy enough in a small dimensional case, but the marginalization
grows exponentially with the number of possibly-zero variates.

For example, with:

  Y ~ normal(d1 * b1 * X1 + d2 * b2 * X2,
             sigma);

you can marginalize out the indicator variables d1 and d2
based on their probabilities of being included, p_d1 and p_d2.
Hang on, it's ugly.

   parameters {
     real<lower=0,upper=1> p_d1;
     real<lower=0,upper=1> p_d2;
   }
   model {
     real log_p_12;
     real log_p_1;
     real log_p_2;
     real log_p;
     log_p_12 <- log(p_d1)   + log(p_d2);
     log_p_1  <- log(p_d1)   + log1m(p_d2);
     log_p_2  <- log1m(p_d1) + log(p_d2);
     log_p    <- log1m(p_d1) + log1m(p_d2);

     for (n in 1:size(Y)) {
       real log_p[4];
       log_p[1] <- log_p_12 + normal_log(Y[n], b1 * X1[n] + b2 * X2[n], sigma);
       log_p[2] <- log_p_1  + normal_log(Y[n], b1 * X1[n],              sigma);
       log_p[3] <- log_p_2  + normal_log(Y[n], b2 * X2[n],              sigma);
       log_p[4] <- log_p_   + normal_log(Y[n], 0,                       sigma);
       lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log_p);
     }
   ...

where the built-in function log_sum_exp is defined as:

   log_sum_exp(xs) == log(sum(exp(xs));

It's faster more arithmetically stable than the direct implementation.

There's not a good way to vectorize over the data items Y[n],
so it's really inefficient on a per-iteration basis compared
to doing discrete sampling.  Having said that, it should still
work in Stan, and it may wind up giving you higher effective
sample sizes per iteration than sampling the discrete variable.

It would be possible to calculate all of this in a loop, but
I thought it'd be easier to understand blown out.  It won't
be any more efficient in a loop.

For some other alternatives, see the following blog post
and discussion:

http://andrewgelman.com/2013/03/18/tibshirani-announces-new-research-result-a-significance-test-for-the-lasso/

> d1,d2 and d3 are binary variables that turn on or off the contribution of the variables X1, X2 and X3, respectively. If
> we model them as Bernouilli distributions, then the posterior mean of the parameters gives us the probability that the
> variable Xi should be included in the model.
>

> The second example is a state-space model. We can consider for example, a stochastic volatility model, with
> |
> Y[n]~normal(mu,exp(h[n]/2))

> h[n]~h[n-1]+J*hnoise
> hnoise~normal(0,sigmah)
> |
> In this case, J is again a binary variable. If J=0, then h remains the same as in the previous period, while if J=1,

> then (log) volatility changes by the amount hnoise

This one's much easier because the mixture is at the data item level.
But do you really mean it doesn't move at all if J = 0?  If so, then
you get this:

   parameters {
     real<lower=0,upper=1> lambda;
     ...
   }
   model {
     for (n in 2:N) {
       if (h[n] == h[n-1])
         lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log(1 - lambda),
                                    log(lambda) + normal_log(h[n],h[n-1],sigmah));
       else
         lp__ <- lp__ + log(lambda) + normal_log(h[n],h[n-1],sigmah);
     }
     ...
   }

where log_sum_exp(x,y) = log(exp(x) + exp(y)).

I think that captures the model, but someone should doublecheck
my work here.  The above model has a log likelihood equivalent
to:

log PROD_n (
              lambda * Normal(h[n] | h[n-1], sigmah)
              + (1 - lambda) * h[n] == h[n-1]
            )

- Bob

On the other hand, sparse products are indeed an order of magnitude faster (especially with spatial distributions) and optimizing the order of the areas can further improve computation speed; see the attached graph of the pre- and post-optimized spatial matrix (using Matlab's -symrcm- function).

On Wednesday, April 24, 2013 7:27:39 PM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:
> The distribution indeed requires the Kronecker product, so I've followed Ben's suggestion and programmed it element by element. It's not fast, but will have to do for the time being ;) Thank you for taking a look!

Glad it is somewhat functional. In a case like a multivariate normal, you might be able to speed it up a little bit by being clever with the products. So, if you need (in R notation)

t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y

you end up repeatedly post-multiplying Lambda by segments of y and scaling those by elements of D - a * W. Particularly if D - a * W is sparse, you could squeeze out some efficiency gains by using temporaries.

This is one reason why Stan would need a really good implementation of Kronecker products to realize performance improvements, as opposed to merely having a convenient syntax for using the Kronecker product in Eigen.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
OK, I can see why you want a Kronecker product function after
having to write:

  // MVCAR_prec  <- Kronecker_product( D - A , MVCAR_scale );
     temp <- (D - A);
     for (a in 1:I){
      for (b in 1:4){
        rowNr <- (a-1)*4 +b;
        for (c in 1:I){
         for (d in 1:4){
          colNr <-(c-1)*4 +d;
          MVCAR_prec[rowNr,colNr] <- temp[a,c]*MVCAR_scale[b,d];
     }}}}
   f_star ~ multi_normal_prec( zeros, MVCAR_prec );

I didn't follow all the indexing closely, but after you construct
MVCAR_prec, you can check yourself if it's symmetric:

   for (m in 1:rows(MVCAR_prec))
     for (n in (m+1):cols(MVCAR_prec))
       if (fabs(MVCAR_prec[m,n] - MVCAR_prec[n,m]) > 1e-8)
         print("ASYMMETRY FOUND: m=", m, " n=", n);

If it's close but not exact, you can enforce symmetry by doing
this:

   for (m in 1:rows(MVCAR_prec))
     for (n in (m+1):cols(MVCAR_prec))
       MVCAR_prec[m,n] <- MVCAR[n,m];

As to the second issue, you get a std::bad_alloc when the
runtime can't allocate enough memory.  Can you check how your memory
grows as you run?  I'm really hoping it's not a leak on our side!

One other issue is that you can vectorize (and simplify the code)
that looks like this:

   HC1 ~ normal( HC_const[1] + HC_loading[1] * F[1]  , HC_var[1]);
   HC2 ~ normal( HC_const[2] + HC_loading[2] * F[1]  , HC_var[2]);
   HC3 ~ normal( HC_const[3] + HC_loading[3] * F[1]  , HC_var[3]);

I'd rather see a loop with HC made into a 3D array of vectors,

   for (i in 1:3)
     HC[i] ~ normal(HC_const[i] + HC_loading[i] * F[1], HC_var[i]);

Although our code hasn't caught up with our designs, we plan to
vectorize further so that the above loop could be written as:

   HC ~ normal(HC_const + HC_loading * F[1], HC_var);

You should get some feedback on those with more knowledge of stats
about this choice of prior:

   HC_var ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);

It may be pushing variances to zero a little too firmly.

Also note that the naming is off or you're missing a sqrt, because
Stan parameterizes basic normal() with standard deviation (i.e., scale),
not variance.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 4/30/13 5:56 AM, M.F. Jonker wrote:
> Hi Bob,
>

> 1) I ran the factor model on a workstation with 36 Gb of RAM and STAN throws a bad::alloc error without ever reaching
> more than 2.5 Gb.

Is this through R or on the command line?

Are you sure whatever you're running is running
in 64-bit mode rather than 32-bit mode?  Often with
32-bit mode, you hit memory restrictions around 2GB
(what you can address with 31 bits [32 = 31 + sign]).

> 2) I implemented the asymmetry check in the mortality rate model, and in the first 20/30 iterations there are some
> asymmetries found and some samples rejected. Afterwards, everything sampled fine (I specified a total of 4000
> iterations). The model doesn't properly converge in 4000 iterations, and when I specify 30,000 iterations, I again end
> up with asymmetry-warnings after approximately 8000 iterations. Given that there are several thousands of iterations in
> between without errors , I'm not entirely sure what to do - strictly enforcing symmetry would probably not be necessary
> if I had programmed it correctly, right? But on the other hand, there are thousands of iterations without asymmetry
> problems.

Probably the best thing to do is to enforce symmetry
anyway.  If you can only compute the entries for
(i,j) with i <= j, you can use those to set the values
for i > j.  This is both more efficient computationally
(re-using auto-diff vars) and also avoids lack of symmetry.

Floating point operations are tricky.  Even if the
algebra over real numbers is symmetric, it's not necessarily
going to be the case in a computer implementation.  There
are very simple cases where (a + (b + c)) is not equal to
((a + b) + c).  Or where a, b > 0 and (a + b) == a.
